**The Protestant Reformation Spread**

Efforts to stop Martin Luther did not work.  
His new Christian ideas, called Protestantism, spread across German-speaking lands.  
By the end of the 1500s, it was firmly established in western and central Europe too.  

Many rulers welcomed Protestantism.  
It gave them a reason to reject the pope’s authority.  
Luther urged German princes to do the same.  

The Catholic Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (also King Charles I of Spain) strongly opposed Protestantism.  
But in 1555, the Peace of Augsburg changed things.  
Rulers inside the empire could choose Lutheranism as their official church if they wanted.  
If a ruler chose Lutheranism, his people had to follow it too.  

Many northern German rulers became Lutheran.  
In Austria and Bavaria (southern Germany), Catholic power stayed strong.  
No other religions were allowed in these areas.  

**Zwingli in Switzerland**

In Switzerland, Ulrich Zwingli took Luther’s ideas further.  
He worked in the city of Zurich.  
Zwingli had been a priest.  
He called for big changes:  

* He rejected the Catholic belief that Jesus becomes truly present in communion wine and bread during Mass (transubstantiation). Luther did not go this far.  
* He opposed fasting before holidays.  
* He wanted religious images removed from churches.  
* He banned church organs, closed monasteries and convents, and printed the Bible in German instead of Latin.  
* He ended clerical celibacy (priests could marry).  
* He said the Bible never mentions purgatory.  

Zwingli was killed in 1531 during fighting between Catholic and Protestant areas of Switzerland.  

**The Swiss Brethren and Anabaptists**

Konrad Grebel, a Swiss merchant, agreed with Zwingli’s ideas.  
Grebel especially liked Zwingli’s view that baptism should wait until adulthood.  
This is when a person can choose to turn away from sin.  
Grebel thought Zwingli was reforming too slowly.  
So in 1524, Grebel started his own group: the Swiss Brethren.  

The Swiss Brethren was one of several Anabaptist churches formed in the 1500s.  
Anabaptists are groups that reject infant baptism.  
They only baptize adults who can make their own faith choice.  

Most Catholics and other Protestants baptized babies.  
They believed this removes original sin (the first human mistake by Adam and Eve).  
Anabaptists thought only adults can truly choose faith and deny sin.  
Therefore, only adults should be baptized.  

Because baptism happens only once, an adult rebaptized after infant baptism was breaking Catholic teaching.  

Other Anabaptist groups included the Hutterites, Mennonites, and Amish (who split from Mennonites later).  
All believed in adult baptism.  
They also wanted church and state separate.  
Most were pacifists—they did not want war.  
Because they refused to hold public office, serve in armies, or let rulers control religion, European leaders often feared them.  
Anabaptists were sometimes attacked violently.  

**Calvin in Geneva**

Another center of Protestant thought was Geneva, Switzerland.  
John Calvin led the city’s church.  
Calvin was born Catholic in France but became Protestant while fleeing persecution.  
His ideas agreed with Luther on many points.  
But Calvin taught a key difference: predestination.  

Predestination means God decided long ago who will be saved after death and who will go to hell.  
No one can know for sure if they are saved or damned.  
No human action can guarantee salvation.  

Calvinists accepted this strict idea.  
Even though it denies personal choice, they lived very moral lives.  
They worked hard and were deeply religious.  
They hoped their good behavior showed they were truly chosen for heaven.  
They rejected dancing, public drinking, gambling, and obscene speech.  
A special court called the Consistory could punish such behavior.  

Calvinism spread quickly.  
Followers formed the Dutch Reformed Church in the Netherlands.  
In Scotland, it became the Presbyterian Church.  
In France, Calvinists were called Huguenots.  

**The English Reformation Was Different**

Martin Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, and Anabaptist leaders deeply believed their teachings.  
But the English Reformation was different.  
It started from the top down, not by a personal conversion.  
It began with a king’s practical decision.  

Before 1530, Henry VIII of England seemed devoutly Catholic.  
He even criticized Luther.  
Henry was married to Catherine of Aragon, daughter of Spain’s Ferdinand and Isabella (who had defeated Muslim Granada and expelled Jews and Muslims from Spain).  
Catherine and Henry had only one living child: a daughter, Mary.  

Although English law allowed queens to inherit the throne, Henry wanted a clear male heir.  
He feared challenges to his son’s future rule.  
Henry wanted a wife who could give him sons.  

Against Catherine’s wishes, Henry asked the pope to annul his marriage.  
An annulment means a marriage is declared never valid—not a divorce, which the Catholic Church does not allow.  
Henry argued that because Catherine had previously married his dead older brother, her marriage to him was invalid under church law.  

The pope refused the annulment.  
Henry then declared English churches no longer obeyed the pope.  
In 1534, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy.  
This made the English monarch head of the Church of England (also called Anglican Church).  
The archbishop of Canterbury finally granted Henry’s annulment.  
Henry had already secretly married Anne Boleyn in time to see her give birth to Elizabeth (later Queen Elizabeth I).  

Under Henry, the Church of England stayed mostly Catholic in beliefs and rituals.  
He closed English monasteries.  
But he did not remove all Catholic practices.  
This upset many Protestants.  

After Henry’s death, his son Edward VI became king.  
Edward was still a child, so regents ruled.  
They made the Anglican Church more Protestant, with Edward’s agreement.  
Priests were allowed to marry.  
Using rosary beads in prayer was banned.  
Church processions stopped.  
Statues and stained-glass windows were removed from churches.  
The mass service was reformed, removing many Catholic rituals.  
In 1549, the English *Book of Common Prayer* set out the new church service.  
Ministers who refused to use this book could be fired or imprisoned.

**The Protestant Reformation Spread**

Efforts to stop Martin Luther did not work.  
His new Christian ideas, called Protestantism, spread across German-speaking lands.  
By the end of the 1500s, it was firmly established in western and central Europe too.  

Many rulers welcomed Protestantism.  
It gave them a reason to reject the pope’s authority.  
Luther urged German princes to do the same.  

The Catholic Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (also King Charles I of Spain) strongly opposed Protestantism.  
But in 1555, the Peace of Augsburg changed things.  
Rulers inside the empire could choose Lutheranism as their official church if they wanted.  
If a ruler chose Lutheranism, his people had to follow it too.  

Many northern German rulers became Lutheran.  
In Austria and Bavaria (southern Germany), Catholic power stayed strong.  
No other religions were allowed in these areas.  

**Zwingli in Switzerland**

In Switzerland, Ulrich Zwingli took Luther’s ideas further.  
He worked in the city of Zurich.  
Zwingli had been a priest.  
He called for big changes:  

* He rejected the Catholic belief that Jesus becomes truly present in communion wine and bread during Mass (transubstantiation). Luther did not go this far.  
* He opposed fasting before holidays.  
* He wanted religious images removed from churches.  
* He banned church organs, closed monasteries and convents, and printed the Bible in German instead of Latin.  
* He ended clerical celibacy (priests could marry).  
* He said the Bible never mentions purgatory.  

Zwingli was killed in 1531 during fighting between Catholic and Protestant areas of Switzerland.  

**The Swiss Brethren and Anabaptists**

Konrad Grebel, a Swiss merchant, agreed with Zwingli’s ideas.  
Grebel especially liked Zwingli’s view that baptism should wait until adulthood.  
This is when a person can choose to turn away from sin.  
Grebel thought Zwingli was reforming too slowly.  
So in 1524, Grebel started his own group: the Swiss Brethren.  

The Swiss Brethren was one of several Anabaptist churches formed in the 1500s.  
Anabaptists are groups that reject infant baptism.  
They only baptize adults who can make their own faith choice.  

Most Catholics and other Protestants baptized babies.  
They believed this removes original sin (the first human mistake by Adam and Eve).  
Anabaptists thought only adults can truly choose faith and deny sin.  
Therefore, only adults should be baptized.  

Because baptism happens only once, an adult rebaptized after infant baptism was breaking Catholic teaching.  

Other Anabaptist groups included the Hutterites, Mennonites, and Amish (who split from Mennonites later).  
All believed in adult baptism.  
They also wanted church and state separate.  
Most were pacifists—they did not want war.  
Because they refused to hold public office, serve in armies, or let rulers control religion, European leaders often feared them.  
Anabaptists were sometimes attacked violently.  

**Calvin in Geneva**

Another center of Protestant thought was Geneva, Switzerland.  
John Calvin led the city’s church.  
Calvin was born Catholic in France but became Protestant while fleeing persecution.  
His ideas agreed with Luther on many points.  
But Calvin taught a key difference: predestination.  

Predestination means God decided long ago who will be saved after death and who will go to hell.  
No one can know for sure if they are saved or damned.  
No human action can guarantee salvation.  

Calvinists accepted this strict idea.  
Even though it denies personal choice, they lived very moral lives.  
They worked hard and were deeply religious.  
They hoped their good behavior showed they were truly chosen for heaven.  
They rejected dancing, public drinking, gambling, and obscene speech.  
A special court called the Consistory could punish such behavior.  

Calvinism spread quickly.  
Followers formed the Dutch Reformed Church in the Netherlands.  
In Scotland, it became the Presbyterian Church.  
In France, Calvinists were called Huguenots.  

**The English Reformation Was Different**

Martin Luther, Zwingli, Calvin, and Anabaptist leaders deeply believed their teachings.  
But the English Reformation was different.  
It started from the top down, not by a personal conversion.  
It began with a king’s practical decision.  

Before 1530, Henry VIII of England seemed devoutly Catholic.  
He even criticized Luther.  
Henry was married to Catherine of Aragon, daughter of Spain’s Ferdinand and Isabella (who had defeated Muslim Granada and expelled Jews and Muslims from Spain).  
Catherine and Henry had only one living child: a daughter, Mary.  

Although English law allowed queens to inherit the throne, Henry wanted a clear male heir.  
He feared challenges to his son’s future rule.  
Henry wanted a wife who could give him sons.  

Against Catherine’s wishes, Henry asked the pope to annul his marriage.  
An annulment means a marriage is declared never valid—not a divorce, which the Catholic Church does not allow.  
Henry argued that because Catherine had previously married his dead older brother, her marriage to him was invalid under church law.  

The pope refused the annulment.  
Henry then declared English churches no longer obeyed the pope.  
In 1534, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy.  
This made the English monarch head of the Church of England (also called Anglican Church).  
The archbishop of Canterbury finally granted Henry’s annulment.  
Henry had already secretly married Anne Boleyn in time to see her give birth to Elizabeth (later Queen Elizabeth I).  

Under Henry, the Church of England stayed mostly Catholic in beliefs and rituals.  
He closed English monasteries.  
But he did not remove all Catholic practices.  
This upset many Protestants.  

After Henry’s death, his son Edward VI became king.  
Edward was still a child, so regents ruled.  
They made the Anglican Church more Protestant, with Edward’s agreement.  
Priests were allowed to marry.  
Using rosary beads in prayer was banned.  
Church processions stopped.  
Statues and stained-glass windows were removed from churches.  
The mass service was reformed, removing many Catholic rituals.  
In 1549, the English *Book of Common Prayer* set out the new church service.  
Ministers who refused to use this book could be fired or imprisoned.

**Early English Colonization: Funding, Jamestown, and Labor**

English colonists after Roanoke Island used joint stock companies for funding. These were like modern corporations. The companies sold shares to investors. Investors paid money for a share in the company. The company pooled all this money. It used it for colonization efforts in the Americas.  

Shareholders had limited liability. They could not lose more than they invested. They were not legally responsible for company actions. But they could earn large profits if the company succeeded. Limited risk plus possible high profit made these companies appealing. England’s growing merchant class invested heavily. Companies raised huge sums starting in the early 1600s.  

England promoted colonization for religious and political reasons. But private investors controlled funding. This often pushed efforts toward profitable activities.  

In 1606, the Virginia Company received a royal charter. It was named for Queen Elizabeth. She was called the "Virgin Queen" because she never married. The company sent 144 men and boys to North America. In 1607, these settlers founded Jamestown. They named it after King James I. Jamestown was on the Chesapeake Bay in present-day Virginia.  

Many settlers were younger sons of elite families. Their older brothers inherited all property. These younger sons had little future in England. Many other settlers were artisans. This included goldsmiths and jewelers. They were unused to hard physical labor needed to build a colony.  

Settlers at Jamestown followed mercantilism. Mercantilism is the idea that the world’s wealth, measured in gold and silver, is fixed. A gain for one nation means a loss for another. Mercantilist nations expected colonies to export raw materials. Gold and silver were most important. Colonies should then buy goods from the home country. England hoped the Virginia Company would find gold. This would improve England’s trade balance and increase its wealth. Many in Jamestown also hoped to find gold quickly. They thought this could make them rich without hard work or suffering.  

The settlers did not find much gold. The region had little mineral wealth. Instead, they faced great suffering. Causes included bad weather, starvation, disease, political disputes, and conflict with the Powhatan tribe. The tribe was named after its chief. The Powhatans grew to hate newcomers. They saw Europeans bringing disease and violence to their land. During the winter of 1609-1610, called "the starving time," many colonists died. By May 1610, fewer than a hundred remained. The colony had not made a profit. It almost failed completely.  

Early Virginia colonists found success growing tobacco. Hard work in tough conditions was needed. But by 1614, Jamestown exported tobacco to Europe. They earned profits for the Virginia Company. Smoking dried tobacco became a popular habit in Europe.  

Like Spanish colonists, English settlers struggled to grow crops using only their own labor. Instead, they relied heavily on indentured servants. These were European immigrants. They agreed to work 4 to 7 years in exchange for travel to the colony. They also hoped for a new life after finishing service. Up to 100,000 mostly poor men in their twenties came as indentured servants in the 1600s. Many died from disease, exposure, or overwork. Survivors often became comfortable and respected members of settlements. A few even became wealthy planters.  

In 1619, the first Africans arrived in Virginia. At first, they had similar chances to earn freedom and build wealth as European immigrants. Their situation changed quickly. This was part of a trend starting with Spanish and Portuguese ships bringing Africans to the Americas a century earlier. By the mid-1600s, laws in the Americas began treating Africans differently. Policies bound Africans to servitude for life. European indentured servants regained freedom after their term ended.  

Virginia colonists, like those in Mexico, South America, and the Caribbean, needed steady labor. It was hard to get enough indentured servants from Europe. Coercing Europeans would meet strong resistance. Colonists also faced a growing group of poor white former servants. These men were bitter after their service ended. In 1676, they tried to overthrow the colony’s government. Virginia’s leaders solved these problems by making legal differences between people of European and African ancestry. They gave privileges to whites that blacks did not get. Leaders encouraged Europeans to see Africans as inferior. They said Africans were fit only for hard manual labor. ### Revised Chapter (Dyslexia-Friendly & Readable)

Britain’s success in building colonies sometimes led to strong independent nations. Thirteen British colonies in North America later became the United States. This nation grew wealthier and more powerful than Britain itself.

In the early 1600s, British colonies in North America were small trading posts. By the mid-1700s, they had over two million people. Most colonists governed their own daily lives. They had a strong local economy.

Britain followed mercantilism. This meant the empire wanted to control colonial trade for its own profit. To do this, Britain passed several Navigation Acts starting in the late 1600s. These laws limited where colonies could sell goods. They also stopped smuggling. The goal was to give England all colony profits and block other European nations from buying colony goods.

The 1660 Navigation Act listed colonial products. Colonists could only sell these to England or English colonies. They could not sell to Dutch, French, Spanish, or other foreign merchants—even if those merchants offered more money.

These products included furs, tobacco, and sugar. Europe wanted all of them. The list also covered rice, ginger, cotton, and indigo. Indigo and similar plants made dye. English textile makers needed cotton and dye. So, the 1660 Exportation Act also banned exporting English wool. This protected English cloth makers.

Naval stores were another key group. These were materials to build and repair ships for trade and war. They included masts, hemp (for rope), pine pitch (to seal ships), and pine sap (for turpentine). Colonies had to send these only to England.

After arriving in England, colonial goods faced heavy taxes. The government kept this tax money. Colonies received none of it.

The 1663 Navigation Act added another rule. All goods coming *to* the colonies from other countries had to first land in England. They were taxed there before going on to the colonies. This made imported foreign goods more expensive for colonists. Foreign shippers passed the English tax cost onto them.

By the end of the 1600s and into the 1700s, Parliament added more trade limits. Colonies could not make certain goods that England also produced. They could not sell wool or iron goods—at home or in other English colonies. By the mid-1700s, they also could not export beaver hats. Beaver hats were popular in Europe. Colonists actively traded furs. But Parliament forced them to sell only raw furs, not finished hats. Hats sold for more money. This policy limited how wealthy colonists could become.

After the French and Indian War (which ended in 1763), Britain took new actions that angered colonists. Many colonists wanted land west of the Appalachian Mountains. They wanted to farm in the Ohio Valley’s rich soil. New England families were large. Parents struggled to give each child enough land as generations grew. Southern colonies always needed new, fertile land for tobacco farming. Several colonies claimed this western land. At that time, French and their Indigenous allies lived there or traded there.

Britain won the war against France and its Indigenous allies. Colonists expected to settle the Ohio Valley themselves. But Britain’s government did not allow it. They issued the Proclamation of 1763. This law forbade colonists from settling west of the Appalachians. Britain wanted to avoid new wars with Native nations and save money. Many colonists felt this was unfair. They had fought for Britain in the recent war.

Britain also kept troops in North America after the war. The army protected the frontier, regulated trade, and collected taxes. This cost a lot of money. Britain tried to make colonists pay more new taxes. Or they tried harder to collect existing taxes. Colonists often smuggled goods to avoid trade rules. Parliament responded with laws. Smugglers had to be tried in admiralty courts. These courts did not use juries. Many colonists felt this broke promises in the English Bill of Rights, which protected their legal rights.

In 1774, Parliament passed two more acts that deeply upset colonists. First, they gave control of the Ohio Valley to the new British colony of Quebec. Second, they let Quebec keep French civil law and granted religious freedom to Roman Catholics there. Most British colonists were Protestant. They saw this as unfair. They also felt Parliament was taking away their long-standing right to govern themselves.

These actions made many colonists feel Britain no longer respected their interests. Resentment grew stronger. Bloodshed began in 1775. The American colonies declared independence from Britain in 1776.

Western land desire and its outcome (Proclamation) are a distinct section. Tax/troop issues follow logically after the Proclamation.

**Latin America After Independence: Export Economies**

Many Latin American nations became export economies after independence. They wanted to industrialize. But they faced many obstacles.

At the start of the 1800s, progress began.  
Brazil imported steam engines. It built sugar refineries, coffee processors, and textile mills.  
Paraguay built an iron foundry. It started a steamship line.  
Chile opened coal mines. It built sawmills and flour mills.  
Many countries also built rail lines.  

However, they did not become heavily industrialized.  
Their development took another path instead.

Independence itself was part of the problem.  
When Spain and Portugal ruled, merchants disliked trade rules.  
But those rules also made foreign goods very expensive. This protected local crafts.  
After independence, merchants could trade with any country.  
European and U.S. goods flooded in quickly.  
Like India and Egypt, Latin American goods cost more to make or sell than imports.  
They could not make enough for their own people either.  
Brazilians and Chileans saw silver leaving the country instead of being spent at home.

Latin Americans soon understood:  
Growing cash crops like sugar and coffee made more sense than trying to compete with foreign factories.  
These were colonial-era products still in high demand.  
Later in the 1800s, Brazil grew rubber for the same reason. Its vast land and many farm workers supplied raw materials to industrial nations.  

This choice made sense to landowners and politicians.  
But it locked Latin America into selling raw materials.  
These did not earn as much as finished products made from them.

Latin American countries sold large amounts of cash crops to the U.S. and Europe.  
This enriched landowners.  
But earnings never reached (or even matched) what they paid for imports.  
This created serious problems in society.  

Wealthy landowners and city professionals could afford imported factory goods.  
Farm workers could not. This widened the gap between rich and poor.  

Many industrial improvements Latin America made—like mines and railroads—were funded by European and U.S. banks.  
Most equipment, like steam engines, was imported from Europe.  
This left little money for domestic projects, such as building roads or telegraph lines at home.  

Regional wars in the 1800s also hurt industrialization.  
For example, Paraguay fought Uruguay, Brazil, and Argentina from 1864 to 1870 (the War of the Triple Alliance).  
By the war’s end, fighting and disease had killed many Paraguayan people.  

Many forces together made Latin America’s industrialization efforts largely fail.  
The region stayed mainly an exporter of cash crops.  

Railroads were built, but they were short lines.  
They linked inland areas to the coast. Their main purpose was moving raw materials for export.  
No national rail networks like those in the U.S. or Europe developed.  
Electrification happened only in major cities.

**Revised Chapter (Dyslexia-Friendly & Readable)**

*   **Raw material needs grew during the Second Industrial Revolution.** New machines and processes needed specific materials.
*   Factories needed petroleum for engines. They needed natural rubber for valves and tires. Palm oil was used to lubricate machinery. Copper carried heat and electricity well. Silver was used in medicine and photography. Lead made pipes.
*   Coal was very important. It turned iron into steel. It made gas for home heating. It created the electricity that ran machines, lit streets, and powered buildings.
*   Not all industrial nations could make enough of these materials themselves. They needed to get more from other places.
*   New tastes also increased demand for imports. Middle-class families in Europe and the US wanted their daughters to play the piano. This created a big market for ivory (used to make piano keys).
*   Workers needed quick energy, so coffee, tea, and sugar became more popular. Elites and middle-class people filled homes with furniture made from mahogany, rosewood, and ebony.
*   Cotton cloth stayed popular. But after slavery ended in the US, cloth makers could no longer get cheap raw cotton easily from US slave labor. They needed new sources.
*   Industrial nations had to look outside their own borders for materials and markets. They looked toward Africa, Asia, and Pacific islands.
*   To make large profits, they needed to buy or take raw materials at very low prices. Local people in Africa, Asia, and the Pacific would likely not agree to this. It was also unlikely they would choose to buy manufactured goods from industrial nations if they could make similar things themselves.
*   Therefore, business owners and politicians in industrial nations believed they had to gain control of these distant countries. They thought they needed to rule them as part of an empire. Military conquest was often how they took control.
*   Once a colony was secured, markets were set up, and money was invested, imperial powers wanted to protect their holdings. They did not want other industrial nations to take over parts of their colonies. This led them to increase control in their colonies. It also led them to try to take over neighboring regions. For example, Great Britain fought Russia for control of Afghanistan. Why? To stop Russia from getting close to Britain’s most important colony: India.
*   These new colonies were different from earlier European colonies (from the 1500s and 1600s). It was not expected that many Europeans would move to Africa or Asia to live there permanently. The relationship between these colonies and the home country was not the same as in older "settler colonies" where people moved to live.
*   For example, how the US treated the Philippines and Filipinos was very different from how early North American colonists had been treated by Great Britain.
*   Industrial nations planned to use colony resources and workers. They did not plan to settle these places themselves in large numbers.
*   There were some exceptions to this rule. France took control of Algeria in 1830. In 1848, France made Algeria part of France itself. Many French people and other Europeans then moved to coastal areas of Algeria and Tunisia, with government support during the 19th century. Many Europeans also settled in British and Dutch colonies in southern Africa.
*   But these settlement cases were not the usual way imperialism worked. Most colonies were for resources and trade, not for European settlers to live in permanently.

**Cold War Strategies and Tensions**

The Cold War was between the West and the East.  
It happened on many fronts using many strategies.  

Both sides gave aid and technical help to countries.  
These were in Latin America, Asia, and Africa.  
Many of these countries had been European colonies until World War II ended.  

The United States hoped this aid would stop communism.  
It aimed to take away economic reasons for countries to side with the Soviet Union.  

Communism seemed attractive to many poor people.  
It promised that a nation’s wealth would help all its citizens.  
Under communism, people had jobs, housing, education, health care, and public transport.  
The standard of living was lower than in the West.  
But for poor people facing hunger and homelessness with no hope, communism seemed like a good option.  

Both sides used propaganda to support their ideas.  
They also tried to make the other side look bad.  
Propaganda came as literature, images, and films.  

In 1950, the U.S. started Radio Free Europe.  
It broadcast news to Eastern Bloc countries.  
In 1953, Radio Liberty began broadcasting to the Soviet Union.  

The Free Europe Committee printed leaflets and posters.  
This group had American business leaders and lawyers.  
The U.S. government created this group.  
They showed how life was better in democratic, capitalist countries.  
They dropped these from weather balloons over East Germany, Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary.  

Soviet propaganda stressed peace worldwide.  
It praised communist ideas of a classless society.  
In such a society, people are treated equally regardless of race or gender.  
This message strongly appealed to people in Latin America, Africa, and Asia.  
Some African Americans also felt this way.  
They faced racism and segregation in the United States.  
Opponents of the U.S. civil rights movement often called it communist.  

Sometimes propaganda used sports.  
Each side showed off their swimmers, runners, weightlifters, and gymnasts.  
They wanted to prove their system was better.  
News broadcasts watched medal counts closely at Olympic Games.  

Cultural exchanges also happened.  
Soviet ballet dancers toured the United States.  
American jazz musicians and symphony orchestras visited Eastern Bloc countries.  

Both sides showed their technology and new ideas.  
In 1959, U.S. Vice President Nixon showed a model kitchen in Moscow.  
Premier Khrushchev saw it.  
Khrushchev asked if Americans also had machines to put food in mouths and swallow it.  

Both sides raced to control space.  
In 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik.  
This was the first satellite.  
Figure 14.7 shows this event.  
This hurt U.S. pride.  
In 1958, President Eisenhower asked Congress to make a space agency.  
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) began in 1958.  
In 1961, the Soviet Union sent the first astronaut into space.  
In 1969, the United States landed the first humans on the moon.  

Espionage was another important tool.  
The U.S. used the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).  
The CIA started in 1947.  
The USSR used its spy agency, the KGB.  
These agencies watched each other.  
They also planned sabotage and assassinations.  
They made foreign nations unstable.  
They trained fighters.  
They encouraged revolutions to overthrow governments.  
They helped install leaders friendly to their own country.  

For example, the CIA trained Cuban rebels.  
Their goal was to overthrow Fidel Castro’s communist government in 1961.  
The KGB helped Vietnamese communists.  
They did this during the Vietnam War.  

The most dangerous part of competition was nuclear weapons.  
Both sides built huge nuclear arsenals.  
In 1949, the Soviet Union tested an atomic bomb.  
This ended the U.S. monopoly on nuclear weapons.  
In 1952, the United States made a hydrogen bomb.  
Some scientists who worked on the WWII Manhattan Project opposed this step.  
The U.S. tested it on Eniwetok atoll in the Pacific.  
This bomb was one thousand times stronger than the one used on Hiroshima.  
Because of this, the Soviet Union had to make its own hydrogen bomb.  

In the 1950s, both sides made intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs).  
These are long-range missiles.  
Nuclear warheads could now be launched from inside a country or its satellite nations.  
Air forces could no longer stop nuclear attack alone.  
Both Western and Eastern Bloc countries built shelters for possible nuclear war.  
But neither side believed they could win a full nuclear war.  
Both sides came to believe survival depended on massive retaliation.  
This meant having the ability to cause such huge destruction that the other side would never start a war.  
They feared their own annihilation if they attacked first.  
In the United States, this policy was called Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD).  

If nuclear weapons failed to stop war, both sides had large conventional armies.  
They built many battleships, submarines, and fighter jets.  
They spent billions on these.  
This ensured they could fight a traditional war too.

In August 1941, the United States stopped selling oil and gas to Japan. This was a penalty for Japan’s aggression.  

Japan already planned to take resources in the South Pacific. These came from crumbling European colonies and the Philippines. The Philippines were a U.S. colony.  

Japan thought the United States would not fight hard. Japan decided to attack while talks between Tokyo and Washington were still happening.  

The United States wanted Japan to leave China completely. Japan refused. Japan also believed the United States would not agree to more talks. Japanese leaders felt they had to act before it was too late.  

By late November 1941, U.S. intelligence had broken several Japanese codes. They sent warnings to U.S. forces. These warnings said war with Japan was likely. The Philippines were probably the first target.  

Early on the morning of December 7, a Japanese naval group attacked Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. They avoided detection. The attack destroyed or damaged eight battleships and other ships. It also destroyed or damaged about three hundred aircraft. More than two thousand people were killed. Over one thousand others were injured.  

At the same time, Japan attacked U.S. bases in the Philippines, Guam, and Wake Island.  

On December 8, the United States Congress voted. All members agreed to declare war on Japan.  

A few days later, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. Then the United States entered the European war. It fought with the Allies.  

After Pearl Harbor, China joined the Allies too. But China did not fight in Europe.  

U.S. military planners estimated a huge army would be needed. They thought victory might require nine million troops. These troops would form more than two hundred divisions.  

To build this army, the United States started a large recruitment and draft program.  

Later, recruitment included African Americans, women, Native Americans, and thirty-three thousand Japanese Americans.  

Leadership of these troops fell to Dwight D. Eisenhower. He moved quickly up in rank. He became a key aide to Chief of Staff George C. Marshall. Eisenhower also commanded all U.S. forces in Europe.

After World War II ended, most European countries joined either the Western Bloc or the Eastern Bloc. Yugoslavia was different.

**Joseph Stalin died in 1953.**  
He had led the Soviet Union for many years.  

After his death, Georgy Malenkov became leader briefly.  
Then Nikita Khrushchev took over as leader of the Soviet Union.  

Khrushchev was a strong opponent of the Western Bloc (countries allied with the United States).  
He had once said communism would “bury” capitalism, like Stalin did.  
But Khrushchev also wanted to change some Soviet policies towards the United States and the future direction of the country.  

In February 1956, at the Twentieth Congress of the Soviet Communist Party, Khrushchev criticized Stalin.  
He accused Stalin of serious crimes against the Soviet people.  
This began a major process called de-Stalinization.  

Under de-Stalinization, the Soviet Union changed many Stalin-era rules:  
* Censorship of art and literature was reduced.  
* Many people who had been jailed by Stalin for political reasons were released.  
* Special courts that had convicted these people were dissolved.  
* Public buildings no longer bore Stalin’s name.  
* Monuments to Stalin were taken down.  

These changes in the Soviet Union encouraged similar hopes in other Eastern Bloc countries (countries under Soviet influence).  

In June 1956, workers in Poznan, Poland, protested.  
They marched because of food shortages and poor housing.  
Other cities also saw protests later that year.  
The protests had a strong national feeling.  
People called for the Soviet army to leave Poland.  
They also wanted Russian language classes removed from Polish schools.  

In October 1956, Władysław Gomułka became leader of the Polish Communist Party and thus Prime Minister of Poland.  
Gomułka supported government reforms.  

Soviet leaders worried that Polish reforms might weaken Soviet control over Poland.  
Khrushchev sent Soviet troops toward Warsaw, the capital city.  
He also flew to Poland himself.  
After Gomułka promised he would keep communism and Poland’s ties to the USSR, Khrushchev agreed to let reforms happen.  

As a result:  
* Forced collective farming in Polish agriculture ended.  
* Soviet advisers left Poland.  
* Political prisoners were released.  
* The Roman Catholic Church was given more freedom.  

The success of reforms in Poland encouraged people in Hungary.  

On October 23, 1956, students marched in Budapest, Hungary.  
They demanded several things:  
* Removal of Stalinist symbols.  
* Better wages.  
* Economic changes.  
* Soviet troops to leave Hungary.  

The State Security Police fired at students outside the main radio station.  
Several students were killed.  
This led to a major uprising across Budapest.  
Angry citizens fought police and Soviet soldiers.  
Protesters attacked the parliament building.  
Ernő Gerő, head of Hungary’s ruling party and leader, fled with Prime Minister András Hegedüs.  

Imre Nagy, a reformer, became the new Prime Minister.  
Nagy wanted more than just internal reforms while staying loyal to Moscow.  
On October 28, he called for a cease-fire.  
He dissolved the State Security Police.  
He demanded Soviet troops leave Budapest immediately.  

On November 1, Nagy announced:  
Hungary would no longer be a member of the Warsaw Pact (a Soviet military alliance).  
Hungary would stay neutral in international affairs.  

Three days later, Soviet forces entered Hungary again.  
Soviet leaders may have felt threatened by Hungary’s plan to be neutral.  
They may have wanted to show strong control to other conservative communists.  
Some think the West not intervening made Khrushchev bolder.  

The uprising ended on November 10.  
About 2,500 Hungarians were killed.  
The communist government was re-established under János Kádár.  
Around twenty thousand people were arrested.  
Approximately 200,000 Hungarians fled the country.  
Soviet troops remained permanently in Hungary.  
Imre Nagy was tried and executed in 1958.  

The United States did not get involved in the Hungarian uprising.  
Khrushchev later mocked this decision.  
But the U.S. could not ignore another Soviet demand after this: about West Berlin.  

West Berlin was the capitalist (non-communist) part of divided Berlin.  
Its prosperity made people in East Berlin (the communist part) feel unhappy.  
The freedom there also let many people from East Germany and other Eastern Bloc countries escape to the West.  

This upset Khrushchev.  
West Berlin felt like a problem for him, or a “thorn.”  

In 1958 and again in 1961, Khrushchev demanded that Britain, France, and the United States leave West Berlin.  
These demands were not accepted by the Western countries.  

Later, East German troops built a barrier on August 12–13, 1961.  
They started with barbed wire to divide West Berlin from East Berlin.  
In the following days, they added cement walls to stop crossing between east and west.  

On October 22, 1961, a dispute happened over U.S. officials traveling in Berlin.  
Agreements made at the Potsdam Conference (end of WWII) said Allied forces could move freely in Berlin.  
The United States sent cars with U.S. government employees across the divide to test if Soviets would stop them.  
If stopped, U.S. troops—sometimes in tanks—escorted the cars through.  

On October 27, the Soviet Union responded.  
They sent their own tanks to the entrance of East Berlin.  
U.S. and Soviet tanks pointed their guns at each other.  
A direct fight was avoided when both President Kennedy and Khrushchev agreed: remove all tanks from that spot at the same time.  

Tensions rose again in Europe in 1968, this time in Czechoslovakia.  
Early in the year, conservative leader Antonín Novotný was replaced by Alexander Dubček.  
Dubček started economic reforms.  
He ended government censorship of media and art.  
As Czech people asked for even more changes, Soviet leaders became worried.  
They remembered what happened in Poland and Hungary in 1956.  
Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev feared reforms in Czechoslovakia might cause unrest elsewhere in the Eastern Bloc or within Soviet republics themselves.  
He also believed the United States would not intervene, as it had not before.  

On August 20, 1968, Soviet forces invaded Czechoslovakia.  
By early 1969, resistance had ended.  
The Soviet Union replaced Dubček with conservative Gustáv Husák.  
Husák reversed all of Dubček’s reforms.  
Censorship returned.  
Government control increased again.  

For the Soviets, this invasion showed success of the Brezhnev Doctrine.  
This doctrine promised to help any communist government facing a threat of being overthrown by reformers or others inside it.

### Industrial Cities and Art: A Clear Look

Industrial cities were places where people lived, worked, and spent their free time. They were also subjects in late 19th-century art and books. Industrialization changed how things were made and moved. It also shaped the culture of that time—especially art and literature.

#### Romanticism: Feeling and Nature (Late 1700s–Early 1800s)
The first big cultural reaction to industry began in the late 1700s and early 1800s. This movement was called **romanticism**.  
Romantic artists and writers valued strong feelings and imagination. They often chose nature, ordinary people, exotic places, old history, or supernatural themes for their work.  
Romantics wrote about the beauty and great power of nature. They also criticized cities and industrial growth. They felt these things harmed people and the natural world.  
Poet William Blake called England’s factories "dark satanic mills." This phrase shows how romantics saw modern industry: powerful, evil, and damaging to people’s spirits. (Note: "Satanic" here means seeming evil or destructive, not a religious statement about actual Satan.)

#### Realism: Life as It Really Is (19th Century)
Another important movement in the 1800s was *realism*.  
Realists focused on everyday life in their own time. They did not look to exotic places, old history, or distant lands like romantics often did.  
Realists showed life exactly as it was—even the hard or ugly parts. Some realist painters, like Rosa Bonheur and Jean-François Millet, chose rural scenes: horse fairs in the country, oxen pulling plows, men sowing fields.  
Other realist artists turned to modern cities. John Sloan and George Luks painted inside city bars and busy streets in working-class neighborhoods. They showed real people in real places.

#### Realism in Writing: Charles Dickens and Others
Writers also used the city as their main subject. One of the greatest realist writers was Britain’s Charles Dickens.  
In his many popular novels, Dickens showed the tough lives of poor, working-class, and middle-class city people. He set scenes in foundling homes (places for orphaned children), prisons, poor neighborhoods, and dark city streets.  
Some critics said Dickens made the poor seem too perfect or "virtuous" in his books. But his honest writing—and his calls for change—helped people understand problems, especially for children. This raised awareness and led to some social improvements.  
Other writers focused even more on difficult lives.  
*   Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoyevsky wrote about St. Petersburg’s streets, poor neighborhoods where the very poor lived, and cheap bars where people tried to escape their problems.  
*   French writer Honoré de Balzac often told stories about crime and seedy parts of French cities.  
*   Gustave Flaubert, also French, wrote *Madame Bovary*. This story is about a young doctor’s wife in the countryside who wants city goods and pleasures too much. Her desire leads to her ruin.  
*   American writer Kate Chopin wrote about women who felt trapped by marriage and social rules of the time. She showed their quiet struggles.

#### Naturalism: Environment Shapes People (Late 19th Century)
In the late 1800s, *naturalism* grew from realism.  
Naturalist writers showed characters in a cold, detached way. They argued that people’s lives are strongly shaped by where they live and their family background (heredity). Often, characters act in ways they cannot fully control because of these forces.  
French novelist Émile Zola created naturalism. His books show people trapped by their surroundings or birth into behaviors they cannot choose freely.  
For example, in *Thérèse Raquin* (published in 1867), the main character is an orphan. The woman who raised her forces Thérèse to marry her sickly son—a man Thérèse does not love. Later, with help from a rough man she feels drawn to, Thérèse murders him. Literary critics were shocked by this story and later naturalist works. They called them immoral. But Zola argued society caused the characters’ actions.

#### Naturalism in America: *McTeague* (1899)
American readers were also shocked by *McTeague*, a 1899 novel by Frank Norris.  
The story is about McTeague, a dentist. He marries Trina, who his friend loved. The friend ruins McTeague’s dental business as revenge. This forces McTeague to run away after stealing money from Trina. When he returns with nothing left, Trina refuses to help him. In anger, McTeague beats her to death. He then flees the law, with his former friend chasing him.  
The novel ends with McTeague alone in the desert, handcuffed to his dead friend’s body.  
In *McTeague*’s world, people are shown as greedy, unfaithful, and violent. There seems to be no escape from life’s harsh realities. Critics felt this view was very bleak, but Norris argued it showed true human nature under difficult conditions.

### Industrial Cities and Art: A Clear Look

Industrial cities were places where people lived, worked, and spent free time. They were also subjects in late 19th-century art and books. Industrialization changed how things were made and moved. It also shaped culture of that time—especially art and literature.

#### Romanticism: Feeling and Nature (Late 1700s–Early 1800s)  
The first big cultural reaction to industry began in the late 1700s and early 1800s. This movement was called **romanticism**. *Romanticism means artists and writers valued strong feelings, imagination, and nature.*  
Romantics often chose nature, ordinary people, exotic places, old history, or supernatural themes for their work.  
Romantics wrote about the beauty and great power of nature. They also criticized cities and industrial growth. They felt these things harmed people and the natural world.  
Poet William Blake called England’s factories "dark satanic mills." *This phrase means Blake saw modern industry as powerful, evil-seeming, and damaging to people’s spirits.* (Note: "Satanic" here describes seeming evil or destructive, not a religious statement about actual Satan.)

#### Realism: Life as It Really Is (19th Century)  
Another important movement in the 1800s was *realism*. *Realism means artists and writers showed everyday life exactly as it was—including hard or ugly parts.*  
Realists did not look to exotic places, old history, or distant lands like romantics often did.  
Some realist painters, like Rosa Bonheur and Jean-François Millet, chose rural scenes: horse fairs in the country, oxen pulling plows, men sowing fields.  
Other realist artists turned to modern cities. John Sloan and George Luks painted inside city bars and busy streets in working-class neighborhoods. They showed real people in real places.

#### Realism in Writing: Charles Dickens and Others  
Writers also used the city as their main subject. One of the greatest realist writers was Britain’s Charles Dickens. *Charles Dickens wrote novels about poor, working-class, and middle-class city people.*  
In his many popular novels, Dickens showed the tough lives of these groups. He set scenes in foundling homes (places for orphaned children), prisons, poor neighborhoods, and dark city streets.  
Some critics said Dickens made the poor seem too perfect or "virtuous" in his books. But his honest writing—and his calls for change—helped people understand problems, especially for children. This raised awareness and led to some social improvements.  
Other writers focused even more on difficult lives:  
*   Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoyevsky wrote about St. Petersburg’s streets, poor neighborhoods where the very poor lived, and cheap bars where people tried to escape their problems.  
*   French writer Honoré de Balzac often told stories about crime and seedy parts of French cities.  
*   Gustave Flaubert, also French, wrote *Madame Bovary*. This story is about a young doctor’s wife in the countryside who wants city goods and pleasures too much. Her desire leads to her ruin.  
*   American writer Kate Chopin wrote about women who felt trapped by marriage and social rules of the time. She showed their quiet struggles.

#### Naturalism: Environment Shapes People (Late 19th Century)  
In the late 1800s, *naturalism* grew from realism. *Naturalism means writers showed characters shaped strongly by where they live and family background (heredity). Often, characters act in ways they cannot fully control because of these forces.*  
French novelist Émile Zola created naturalism. His books show people trapped by their surroundings or birth into behaviors they cannot choose freely.  
For example, in *Thérèse Raquin* (published in 1867), the main character is an orphan. The woman who raised her forces Thérèse to marry her sickly son—a man Thérèse does not love. Later, with help from a rough man she feels drawn to, Thérèse murders him. Literary critics were shocked by this story and later naturalist works. They called them immoral. But Zola argued society caused the characters’ actions.

American readers were also shocked by *McTeague*, a 1899 novel by Frank Norris. *McTeague is about a dentist named McTeague.*  
The story begins with McTeague marrying Trina, who his friend loved. The friend ruins McTeague’s dental business as revenge. This forces McTeague to run away after stealing money from Trina. When he returns with nothing left, Trina refuses to help him. In anger, McTeague beats her to death. He then flees the law, with his former friend chasing him.  
The novel ends with McTeague alone in the desert, handcuffed to his dead friend’s body.  
In *McTeague*’s world, people are shown as greedy, unfaithful, and violent. There seems to be no escape from life’s harsh realities. Critics felt this view was very bleak, but Norris argued it showed true human nature under difficult conditions.

**Labor Systems After Slavery Ended**

Slavery and serfdom ended in most industrialized countries during the 1800s. But people still needed workers for farms and factories. Two systems remained to get long-term labor: work contracts and debt bondage. Both are still used today in some places.

*   **Work Contracts:** People sign an agreement. They promise to do a job for a set time or fee. This is called contract labor. A specific type is indentured servitude. In this, people agree to work for a fixed period. Their employer controls most of their daily life during that time. They cannot leave early. But unlike slavery, the contract has an end date.
*   **Debt Bondage:** A person owes money. To pay back the debt, they (or someone else) must work for the lender. The work continues until the debt is fully paid with labor. Indentured servitude and debt bondage were common in the late 1800s. They are similar but different from slavery because, in theory, the work period ends.

**Examples Around the World**

*   **United States:** Work contracts (indentured servitude) were common when America was young. Many Europeans came to America by agreeing to work for several years. This ended mainly by the mid-1800s. But it continued in some areas. In Hawaii, plantation owners hired contract workers from Portugal, China, Korea, Japan, and the Philippines, especially for sugarcane.
*   **Chinese Workers in the U.S.:** Many Chinese immigrants came as debt laborers. They did not sign a contract directly with an American employer. Instead, they paid a company (often the Six Companies, a Chinese business) to bring them to America. They had to work to pay back this cost before returning home.
*   **Other Places:** After slavery ended, other countries used work contracts too. Australia brought indentured workers from Pacific islands like the Solomon Islands, Tuvalu, Samoa, and Kiribati. Britain, France, and others sent Chinese and Indian workers to Latin America, the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and African colonies. These workers were paid very little. They worked long hours. They faced harsh punishment. They received only enough food to survive. Reports of their bad treatment led some countries to stop this trade. Britain stopped its ships from carrying Asian workers to Cuba and Peru. In 1874, Portugal stopped the trade through Macao, a colony often used to send Chinese workers elsewhere.
*   **Debt Bondage Examples:** Debt bondage was also widespread in the late 1800s. In Japan during the 1880s, some families facing poverty "rented" their daughters to factories. The girls got food and shelter. Their earnings went home to help their parents. Some girls were sent to brothels; some chose this themselves to protect their family.
*   **Debt Bondage in the U.S.:** Southern American farmers used debt bondage to keep workers (both African Americans and poor White people) on their land. It also trapped many Asian laborers in South America, even after their original contracts ended.
*   **Hard-to-Escape Debt:** Sharecroppers and tenant farmers worked land owned by others. Before harvest, they bought food and supplies on credit from the landlord’s store. They often needed to rent tools or seeds from the landlord too. After selling their crop, they paid back what they owed. But store prices and interest were often very high. Income from the harvest was usually not enough to cover all debts. The unpaid balance was added to next year’s debt. Some employers paid workers only with scrip—a paper note that could *only* be spent at the landlord’s store. Workers had no choice but to go into debt there. In Japanese brothels, everything the women used—clothing, food—was recorded as a debt. They could not leave until they paid back the original amount plus all costs.

**European Migration: 1800s to Early 1900s**

Many Europeans left their homes between 1800 and 1914. They looked for better work and life elsewhere. About 60 million people made this journey. Most came from rural areas. Southern Italy and Sicily were common places they left.

**To the United States:**  
Around 28 million people went to the US in this time. Most arrived between 1890 and 1914. Many were poor farmers from southern or eastern Europe. Germany and Ireland also sent many immigrants early on. Later, Jews from the Russian Empire came too. They faced strong prejudice and anti-Semitism. Violent attacks called **pogroms (violent attacks where people were hurt or killed and homes destroyed)** forced many to leave. Political opponents and skilled workers displaced by new factories also migrated.

**Other Destinations:**  
After the US, Argentina received about 4.5 million immigrants. At one point, they were 30% of Argentina’s population. Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay also got large numbers. Canada welcomed about 5.1 million people from the 1850s to the 1920s. Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa were common places too. Gold discoveries in Australia (1851) and South Africa (1886) made these places especially popular.

**Jobs Immigrants Did:**  
Immigrants worked in many jobs. Many labored in factories. Jewish immigrants often worked in clothing factories, like in New York City. Polish and other eastern Europeans worked in steel mills (Pittsburgh) or meatpacking plants (Chicago). Portuguese people often fished or worked in textile mills in New England, sometimes with French Canadians. Italians did farm work, mining, and building jobs. Welsh people mined coal in the western US. Irish immigrants worked in mines, built railroads, and in factories across the US. Women from all groups often worked as housemaids or in domestic service.

**How People Reacted:**  
Reactions to immigrants varied by country and background. In the US:  
*   Germans and eastern European Christians might be laughed at for their customs, but were generally accepted.  
*   Irish newcomers (mostly Catholic) faced strong rejection when they arrived in large numbers in the 1840s-1850s. The US was mostly Protestant then. But by the late 1800s, Irish people and their children became politicians, business owners, and police officers.  
*   Jewish immigrants and Italians, who arrived more recently, often faced discrimination. Anti-Semitism (prejudice against Jews) was common.

**Changing Laws:**  
By the end of the 1800s, many native-born US Protestants (especially those from northern Europe) wanted stricter immigration rules. This led to the Johnson-Reed Act in 1924. The law set a total limit on new immigrants *from outside the Western Hemisphere* (like Europe). It also used a quota: only 2% of the people living in the US in 1890 who were from any given country could immigrate now.  
Example: If 100,000 Italians lived in the US in 1890, only about 2,000 new Italian immigrants could be allowed under this rule—even if the total limit for all countries wasn’t reached yet.  
This mattered because most immigrants before 1890 came from northern/western Europe (like England, Ireland, Germany). Fewer came from southern or eastern Europe (like Italy, Poland, Russia). So the 2% rule let far more English, Irish, and German people in than Italian, Polish, or Russian Jewish people.  
The law also banned almost all immigration from Asia (except Filipinos, as the US territory then).

**In Latin America:**  
Things were different there. Argentina and Uruguay had small populations because they lacked gold/silver mines and good climates for sugar/coffee. European immigrants were welcomed as a helpful increase. Brazil and Venezuela actively encouraged European immigrants to join their mostly African, Indigenous, and mixed-race populations. They wanted more people of European descent.

**Unions and Socialism in the 1800s**

In Britain and the United States, unions formed without strong links to political parties.  
In Germany, France, and Russia, unions grew because of political ideas.  
The main idea that shaped these unions was socialism.  

Today, socialism is a political theory. It says the government should own factories, farms, and other places where goods are made.  
Socialism in the 1800s was different. It had many forms.  
But all versions shared three ideas:  
* They disliked pure free-market capitalism (where business owners decide everything).  
* They wanted to improve poor people's lives.  
* They believed government should fix problems caused by industry and factories.  

**Early 1800s: Utopian Socialism**  
In the early 1800s, "utopian socialism" was common. This idea focused on creating a perfect society.  
French thinkers like Henri de Saint-Simon and Charles Fourier wrote about ideal communities.  
They believed in sharing, cooperation, and fairness.  
Some wanted big changes: communal housing, free love, and women's rights. These ideas were radical at the time.  

Some reformers tried to build these communities.  
Robert Owen was a British owner of textile mills (factories that make cloth).  
He tried his ideas in New Lanark, Scotland. This village housed workers from his father-in-law’s mill.  
He also started New Harmony in Indiana, USA.  
In both places:  
* Workers had an eight-hour workday.  
* They lived in decent homes.

**Mid-1800s: Scientific Socialism**  
By the mid-1800s, utopian socialism was less common. "Scientific socialism" became more influential.  
The term was first used by French thinker Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. It meant using reason to plan society.  
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels made this idea famous.  
They wrote *The Communist Manifesto* in 1848. That year, revolutions happened across Europe.  

Because of these revolutions:  
* Men gained or expanded voting rights in France and Prussia (a German region).  
* By the end of the 1800s, men in France and Germany had used their votes to change laws.

**Marx and Engels' Ideas**  
Marx and Engels believed history changes through class struggles.  
In industrial times, the struggle was between:  
* The **bourgeoisie**: factory, mine, and railroad owners who make wealth.  
* The **proletariat**: workers paid low wages whose labor creates that wealth.  

Marx and Engels thought capitalism would end when workers rose up in revolution.  
They would overthrow the owners.  
After this:  
* All people would be equal.  
* All property would belong to everyone.  
* Class divisions and fighting would stop.  

This philosophy is called Marxism. It became the main idea for socialists in the second half of the 1800s.  

Marx never tried to put his ideas into action himself.  
But during the Second Industrial Revolution, many workers used his ideas to form unions and political parties.  
In 1864, socialists started the International Workingmen’s Association (IWA) in London.  
Many types of socialists joined, including Marx.  
Disagreements soon happened over key issues.  

Some socialists thought violence was needed for change.  
Others believed peaceful, democratic methods were better.  
Those who favored peace are often called **social democrats**.

One large and important party was the German Social Democratic Party. It started in 1875.  
Its goals included:  
* Laws to improve workers' lives.  
* Reducing work hours.  
* Helping form trade unions.  
* Passing worker protection laws.  
Many members were elected to parliament.

* The Social Democratic Party of Austria started in 1889.

The French Workers’ Party began in 1880 as an alternative to the FSWF's gradual approach.  
The Russian Social Democratic Labor Party formed in 1898, uniting smaller socialist groups.  
The Socialist Revolutionary Party started in Russia in 1902. It focused on peasants (farmers), not just factory workers. It used violence, like assassinating officials.  
Most Russian socialists who followed traditional Marxist ideas joined the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party when it formed in 1898.  
A revolutionary group within this party, the Bolsheviks, took control of Russia in 1917.

Socialists also disagreed about government’s role in building socialism.  
Marx said government would disappear once equality was reached and class fighting ended.

Some socialists worried this new government would become a new group of rulers who oppress people.  
They believed all government should end. This idea is called **anarchism**.  
A leading anarchist was Mikhail Bakunin, a Russian revolutionary.  
Bakunin joined the IWA in 1868.  
He strongly disagreed with Marx about government’s role.  
At the IWA’s Fifth Congress in 1872, his views led to his removal from the group.  

**Opposition to Socialism and Anarchism**  
Business owners, middle-class, and upper-class people generally opposed socialism and anarchism.  
They believed business owners provide goods and services at fair prices.  
This helps the economy grow and keeps their country strong.  
They thought they deserved fair profit for taking financial risks in business.  
To keep prices low and earn profit, they could not pay high wages to workers.  

Opponents argued further:

**Revised Chapter: Civilian Life During WWI**

Many civilians supported the war effort. Others opposed the war or questioned why it started. Disapproval grew as the war continued and food became scarce. Home front morale fell.

In Germany, soldiers got food first. Civilians often had little to eat. This was hardest for the elderly and people not working in war jobs. The British blockade of Germany (1914-1918) made things worse. Bread rationing began in Germany in 1915. The winter of 1916-1917 was very cold. Much of the potato crop failed. Tens of thousands ate only turnips. Food shortages caused food riots in Germany from 1915 onward.

Food shortages also happened in Austria-Hungary. Its transport system was less developed than Germany's. Moving food was harder. Like Germany, it prioritized soldiers' food over civilians'. Food supply problems made some civilians doubt the government. It hurt morale at home.

Civilian unhappiness rose as more young men were needed for armies. The war lasted a long time. Early excitement in 1914 faded. Some recruits doubted their army could win. They questioned if risking their lives was worth it. Others, called conscientious objectors, refused to fight for religious or moral reasons. Many young people began questioning the value of fighting for imperial glory.

Canada had a conscription crisis in 1917. Britain needed more troops. Canada used a draft (conscription) to get soldiers. The military stopped a protest in Quebec City. They fired at protesters. Several people died.

Governments used censorship to control civilian views. Censorship limited what news people saw about the war. Newspapers gave vague battle reports. Governments showed pro-war posters and comments. Censorship started in all fighting nations in 1914. The U.S. began it in 1917 when it entered the war.

The U.S. government created the Committee on Public Information. It made pro-war speeches and posters. These were very effective. Most posters showed German troops as dangerous monsters. They claimed Germans would attack the U.S. if not stopped.

The U.S. began stricter rules to stop anti-war speech in 1917. The Espionage Act limited what could be mailed. It banned anti-war newspapers or pamphlets. In 1918, Congress passed the Sedition Act. This law forbade "disloyal, profane, scurrilous, and abusive" words about:  
* Why the U.S. entered the war  
* The draft (military conscription)  
* The American flag  
* Soldiers' uniforms  

The law did not care if statements were true. It cared if they seemed disloyal. Anti-war speech was seen as seditious. **Revised Chapter (Dyslexia-Friendly & Readable):**

After World War I in the 1920s, major governments generally supported disarmament. They limited military buildup. There was great hope for peaceful decades ahead. Many agreements in the 1920s showed this wish for goodwill between nations.

In 1921, the Washington Naval Conference began. It addressed a naval arms race before and during World War I. U.S. Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes proposed an idea. He suggested Britain, the United States, and Japan each destroy some ships. They would also limit future ship building.

The Five-Power Treaty resulted from this conference. The treaty limited warship construction. It also set size limits for aircraft carriers, which were new types of naval ships at that time. The treaty set rules for how many warships each country could have. Britain and the United States could build equal numbers of warships. Japan could build fewer: three warships for every five Britain or the United States built. France and Italy could build even fewer than Japan: 1.75 ships for every five Britain or the U.S. built. Britain and the United States were allowed more ships. This was because they had fleets in both the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean to protect their colonies.

By the late 1920s, optimism was high. People hoped war’s pain might be over. In this spirit, the Kellogg-Briand Pact was created. It was agreed by U.S. Secretary of State Frank Kellogg and French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand. The pact renounced war as a tool of national policy. Fifteen nations signed it in 1928. Over the next years, forty-seven more nations joined. However, there was no way to enforce the pact. There were no penalties for countries that did not follow its ideals. Therefore, the pact did little to stop aggressive military actions by many nations in the following decade.

The same was true of the League of Nations. The League had high ideals. It could issue statements, restrictions, or condemnations. But it could not force other countries to limit their activities. Trade restrictions might have a small effect. However, the League had no military force. It could not physically intervene in any member country’s actions. Thus, as the 1930s began, the League was regularly challenged by aggressive acts worldwide. It had little power to influence these events.

Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931. Italy invaded Libya in 1931 and Ethiopia in 1935. The League protested these invasions, especially the attack on Ethiopia. But it could do very little beyond imposing economic sanctions against Italy. Even these sanctions were not followed by all countries. It became clear that the League had no real power. No country needed to fear its actions.

The government talked about building a worker’s paradise. Reality did not always match this promise. Some things did improve. More people could read and write. Electricity reached many rural areas. Some people got new chances for advancement that were impossible under the tsar.

**Post-War Europe: Reconstruction, Justice, and Displacement (Dyslexia-Friendly Version)**

Spain and Portugal had right-wing dictatorships during the war. They did not join the fighting. Because they stayed out of the conflict, they avoided Allied repair work in their own countries. Fascism suffered a major defeat across Europe, however.

The Soviet Union took back many things from Germany after the war. They removed and moved to the USSR anything useful for rebuilding Soviet industry, which the war had destroyed. This left the Soviet occupation zone – which became East Germany – with little to rebuild itself. The western Allies (Britain, USA, France) began repairing German industry in their own zones. Stalin saw this as greed. He thought it showed continued capitalist hostility to socialism and Western plans to control the world economy.

The Allied powers also wanted justice for war crimes. In August 1945, Britain, the Soviet Union, and the United States agreed to start the International Military Tribunal. This was called the Nuremberg Trials. They were held from 1945 to 1946. The trials dealt with Germans accused of war crimes, crimes against peace, and crimes against humanity. Twenty-two individuals and seven Nazi organizations were charged. Nineteen defendants were found guilty. Sentences ranged from 15 years in prison to death by hanging. Three Nazi organizations were declared criminal groups.

A huge task remained: returning displaced people to their homes. Millions of people had been moved around Europe by the Germans. Some were forced to work in Germany. Others, including many Jewish people, were sent to concentration or death camps. The Soviet Union demanded the return of all its citizens who were still in occupied areas.

The Allies agreed to a plan called Operation Keelhaul. This forcibly returned people who had worked against the Soviets for Germany. Groups included Cossacks, Ukrainians, and Russians. These people were sent back to the USSR. They faced a high risk of harsh treatment, possibly death. Millions of other displaced people were also moved back to their original countries at war's end. For example, Germans living in areas now part of Poland were forced to leave for Germany. The hope was this would reduce ethnic tensions and prevent future conflict.

At the same time, about 250,000 Jewish Holocaust survivors stayed in displaced persons camps. Their home countries refused to take them back. Around 80,000 eventually moved to the United States. Over 100,000 settled in the British Mandate of Palestine. Many displaced people found it hard to return home or find a new safe place.

**Cambodia After 1975**  
Peace came to Vietnam in 1975. But in neighboring Cambodia, a terrible time began.  
Cambodia had stayed neutral during most of the Vietnam War.  
In 1970, Prince Sihanouk was removed from power by General Lon Nol. Lon Nol supported the United States.  
Sihanouk then joined the Cambodian communist group, the Khmer Rouge.  
After years of fighting, the Khmer Rouge took over the government of Lon Nol in 1975.  

Under leader Pol Pot—who admired Mao Zedong—the Khmer Rouge tried to build Cambodia as a perfect communist state.  
They took private property.  
They forced city people to move to the countryside.  
People had to work in labor camps or on collective farms.  
Many died from disease or hunger.  
People who could not work were killed.  

The Khmer Rouge also deliberately tried to kill specific groups:  
* Professionals and intellectuals (including people who wore glasses).  
* Christians, Muslims, and Buddhist monks.  
* People of Chinese, Thai, or Vietnamese background.  

By the time Vietnam invaded Cambodia in 1978 and ended the killings, about three million people had died. That is about one-quarter of Cambodia’s population at that time.  

**Cold War Changes in the West**  
Southeast Asia remained violent after 1975. But hope for peace grew in the West as the Cold War began to ease.  
In 1972, the United States and USSR signed SALT (Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty). This limited weapons development, especially anti-ballistic missile systems. It made mutual assured destruction less useful as a strategy.  
This start marked a period called *détente*. Détente means less tension between the US and USSR. It included trade deals and more arms talks.  

In 1975, the US, USSR, Canada, and all European countries except Albania signed the Helsinki Accords.  
The US and its allies agreed to respect Eastern Bloc borders and not interfere in their internal affairs.

**African Independence After World War II (Dyslexia-Friendly Version)**

After World War II, many African peoples wanted to end Western control. They remembered a 1941 promise called the Atlantic Charter. It said all people should have self-determination – the right to choose their own government. African countries wanted this promise kept true.

In October 1945, leaders from Africa, the Caribbean, India, Sri Lanka, and Central America met in Manchester, England. This was the Fifth Pan-African Congress. They called for an end to colonialism.

European colonial powers did not agree easily. After World War II, they needed resources and markets from colonies to rebuild their damaged economies. For example, Britain gave Gold Coast (later Ghana) a new constitution in 1946. Africans could now elect members to a Legislative Council. But the council could only give advice. Real power stayed with Britain’s appointed governor.

In August 1947, Ghanaians formed the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC). They asked Britain to let Gold Coast govern itself. Kwame Nkrumah was one of its founding members. In January 1948, Nkrumah and another UGCC member spoke to Ghanaian ex-service members. Many were angry about unemployment and inflation. They planned to ask the governor for help. A few days later, riots broke out. The government blamed the UGCC. They arrested several members, including Nkrumah.

In 1949, Nkrumah started his own political party: the Convention People’s Party. In January 1950, he asked his supporters to begin a general strike. This was to force Britain to allow a new constitution. British authorities jailed him again. He was still in prison when Ghana held its first election in 1951. This election allowed all adults to vote – universal suffrage. Nkrumah won. He became prime minister. On March 6, 1957, Ghana gained independence.

Other British colonies also gained independence later. In Kenya, the Kenya African Union (KAU) formed in 1944 to seek freedom from Britain. Jomo Kenyatta became its leader in 1947. Britain refused to grant Kenya independence quickly. White settlers owned many profitable coffee farms and controlled more land than Black Africans.

In 1952, a group called the Mau Mau began fighting for Kenyan independence. The Mau Mau were mainly Kikuyu people. They used violence to achieve their goals. They attacked civilians – both White and Black settlers. They burned homes or killed people with machetes. Africans loyal to Britain were targeted. In response, Britain banned all Kenyan political parties, including the non-violent KAU. Britain also fought back against the Mau Mau. Thousands went to internment camps. Entire villages were moved by force. Innocent civilians were killed by British forces. By 1956, the uprising had largely ended. Britain began talks about Kenyan independence in 1960. Kenya gained independence in 1963. Jomo Kenyatta became prime minister.

Nationalism and the desire for independence were strong in other European colonies too. Some powers offered small changes first. In 1946, France proposed reforms for its African colonies. It ended forced labor and racist laws. It allowed some self-rule. But it did not offer full independence – which is what most Africans wanted and fought for. From 1947 to 1949, the Malagasy Revolt raged in Madagascar. Thousands died. Violence also helped end colonialism in Cameroon in 1957. In Algeria, war lasted from 1954 to 1962. France then granted independence. Over one million people of European descent left Algeria.

In the Belgian Congo (now Democratic Republic of the Congo), Cold War tensions increased violence. In 1960, Belgium promised Congolese independence in thirty years. Nationalist groups like the Congolese National Movement and Alliance of Bakongo demanded immediate independence. Black Congolese held protests that often turned into riots. They refused to pay taxes. Others wanted a communist system. Independence did not end all violence. In 1975, civil war broke out in Angola over control of the country. The United States supported UNITA and FNLA against the MPLA.
