chapter_key: Decolonization in Africa in the Shadow of the Cold War
text:
After world war two ended, many african peoples wanted to end western control.  
Many african peoples remembered a 1941 promise called the atlantic charter.  
The atlantic charter said all people should have self determination.  
Self determination means the right to choose their own government.  
African countries wanted this promise kept true.  

In october 1945, leaders from africa the caribbean india sri lanka and central america met in manchester england.  
This meeting was the fifth pan african congress.  
The leaders called for an end to colonialism.  

European colonial powers did not agree easily.  
After world war two european colonial powers needed resources and markets from colonies.  
The european colonial powers had damaged economies.  
For example, Britain gave gold coast a new constitution in 1946.  
Gold coast later became ghana.  
Africans could now elect members to a legislative council.  
But the council could only give advice.  
Real power stayed with britains appointed governor.  

In august 1947, ghanaians formed the united gold coast convention ugcc.  
The united gold coast convention ugcc asked Britain to let gold coast govern itself.  
Kwame nkrumah was one of the united gold coast convention ugcc founding members.  
In january 1948, Kwame nkrumah and another united gold coast convention ugcc member spoke to ghanaian ex service members.  
Many were angry about unemployment and inflation.  
They planned to ask the governor for help.  
A few days later, riots broke out.  
The government blamed the united gold coast convention ugcc.  
They arrested several members including Kwame nkrumah.  

In 1949, Kwame nkrumah started his own political party the convention peoples party.  
In january 1950, Kwame nkrumah asked his supporters to begin a general strike.  
This was to force Britain to allow a new constitution.  
British authorities jailed Kwame nkrumah again.  
Kwame nkrumah was still in prison when ghana held its first election in 1951.  
This election allowed all adults to vote.  
This is called universal suffrage.  
Kwame nkrumah won.  
Kwame nkrumah became prime minister.  
On march 6 1957, ghana gained independence.  

Other british colonies also gained independence later.  
In kenya, the kenya african union kau formed in 1944 to seek freedom from Britain.  
Jomo kenyatta became the leader of the kenya african union kau in 1947.  
Britain refused to grant kenya independence quickly.  
White settlers owned many profitable coffee farms.  
They controlled more land than black africans.  

In 1952, a group called the mau mau began fighting for kenyan independence.  
The mau mau were mainly kikuyu people.  
The mau mau used violence to achieve their goals.  
They attacked civilians both white and black settlers.  
They burned homes or killed people with machetes.  
Africans loyal to Britain were targeted.  
In response, Britain banned all kenyan political parties.  
This included the non violent kenya african union kau.  
Britain also fought back against the mau mau.  
Thousands went to internment camps.  
Entire villages were moved by force.  
Innocent civilians were killed by british forces.  
By 1956, the uprising had largely ended.  
Britain began talks about kenyan independence in 1960.  
Kenya gained independence in 1963.  
Jomo kenyatta became prime minister.  

Nationalism and the desire for independence were strong in other european colonies too.  
Some powers offered small changes first.  
In 1946, france proposed reforms for its african colonies.  
It ended forced labor and racist laws.  
It allowed some self rule.  
But it did not offer full independence.  
Most africans wanted full independence.  
They fought for it.  
From 1947 to 1949, the malagasy revolt raged in madagascar.  
Thousands died.  
Violence also helped end colonialism in cameroon in 1957.  
In algeria, war lasted from 1954 to 1962.  
France then granted independence.  
Over one million people of european descent left algeria.  

In the belgian congo, now democratic republic of the congo, cold war tensions increased violence.  
In 1960, Belgium promised congolese independence in thirty years.  
Nationalist groups like the congolese national movement and alliance of bakongo demanded immediate independence.  
Black congolese held protests that often turned into riots.  
They refused to pay taxes.  
Many white residents formed armed groups and attacked black people.  
Seeing strong protests, Belgium agreed to give congo independence on june 30 1960.  

Independence did not stop the violence.  
A few days after independence, the white commander of the force publique told black troops that white officers would still be in charge.  
This caused a mutiny by black soldiers.  
Patrice lumumba, leader of the congolese national movement and elected prime minister, replaced the commander.  
He renamed the army the national congo army and promoted black soldiers.  
But the mutiny continued.  
White people were attacked across the country.  
Belgium sent forces to protect white residents.  

At the same time, the congolese mineral rich southern province of katanga declared itself independent.  
Patrice lumumba asked the united nations un peacekeepers to stop this secession.  
The un refused saying it was an internal matter.  
Patrice lumumba then asked the united states for help.  
The us said no.  
Finally he turned to the soviet union which gave weapons and military advice.  
Western countries now saw patrice lumumba as a communist.  
Colonel joseph desire mobuto, head of security, put patrice lumumba under house arrest.  
He placed Joseph kasa vubu, leader of the alliance of bakongo, in charge.  
Later katangese troops killed patrice lumumba.  
The central intelligence agency cia gave money and weapons to colonel joseph desire mobuto and Joseph kasa vubu.  

British politicians saw strong nationalist feelings in africa like in kenya and congo.  
They feared more violence.  
So Britain moved quickly to help its african colonies become independent.  
In 1960, prime minister harold macmillan visited africa.  
He gave a speech called the wind of change.  
He said a wind of change was sweeping africa.  
The time for liberation had come even if some white britons did not want it.  

Portugal refused to give up its colonies.  
Portugals government since 1933 saw the colonies as part of portugal.  
It claimed portugal protected order and civilization in africa.  
Independence movements started in angola, portuguese guinea now guinea bissau, and mozambique like elsewhere in africa.  
Some groups wanted self government like western democracies.  
Others wanted a communist system.  
In angola, Portuguese troops fought the national liberation front fnla mostly rural bakongo people.  
The marxist peoples movement of liberation of angola mpla mainly urban.  
And the national union for the total independence of angola unita mostly rural ovimbundu people.  
In mozambique, the marxist mozambique liberation front fought for independence.  
The african party for the independence of guinea and cape verde led the struggle in guinea bissau.  

The cold war affected these wars.  
The soviet union, china, romania, cuba, and yugoslavia gave aid to independence groups.  
The united states did not because portugal was a nato ally.  
In 1974, leftist military officers overthrew portugals government.  
They set up a democratic government.  
This new government granted independence to angola, guinea bissau, mozambique, cape verde, and sao tome and principe in 1975.  

Independence did not end all violence.  
In 1975, civil war broke out in angola over control of the country.  
The united states supported unita and fnla against the mpla.  

Violence also happened in the former british colony of rhodesia, now zimbabwe.  
White residents rejected britains plan for majority rule.  
They did not want black rhodesians to control the government.  
So in 1965, they declared independence from Britain.  
Ian smith became prime minister.  
Britain opposed this move.  
Civil war started between the white government and two black nationalist groups: the zimbabwe african peoples union zapu led by joshua nkomo.  
And the zimbabwe african national union zanu led by robert mugabe.  
The soviet union supported zapu.  
China supported zanu.  
After years of fighting, an agreement was reached.  
Britain officially recognized zimbabwes independence in 1980.  
Robert mugabe became prime minister.  
Many of joshua nkomo followers were tortured imprisoned or killed until robert mugabe and joshua nkomo merged their parties in 1987.  

In south africa, black africans struggled against white rule.  
This was not a european power but white settlers who had taken over the land.  
In 1910, Britain combined four regions cape colony natal transvaal orange free state into one self governing dominion within the british empire.  
Only white people could vote and govern.  
Power struggles were between british and afrikaner dutch settlers.  
Laws denied black africans voting rights.  
They could not own most land.  
They were forced to live in separate areas called homelands.  
In 1948, these racist laws became formalized as apartheid.  
Apartheid is a system of racial separation.  
In 1950, south africas government passed the suppression of communism act.  
This banned the anti apartheid african national congress anc and pan africanist congress pac plus any actions to end racist laws.  
Therefore, when Britain allowed south africans to vote in 1961 on becoming a republic, most people could not take part.  
Only whites could vote.  

From its start, groups like the african national congress anc and pan africanist congress pac fought apartheid peacefully.  
But after police killed peaceful protesters in sharpeville in 1960 and after the government banned both groups, anc members and pac activists began using sabotage and attacks on police military targets.  
They also used strikes and other non violent actions.  
In 1976, black townships protested a new law forcing black students to learn afrikaans the language of dutch settlers.  
In soweto, police shot at schoolchildren killing over one hundred.  
Over decades, thousands of african national congress anc members and pan africanist congress pac members were arrested and imprisoned including nelson mandela.  
Many were executed.  

By the 1980s, continued resistance against apartheid, economic sanctions from other countries, boycotts of south african businesses, and international criticism began to work.  
In 1991, south africa officially ended apartheid.  
In 1994, the first elections were held where all south africans regardless of race could vote.  
The african national congress anc won the election.  
The new national assembly elected nelson mandela as president.

### Final Year of World War I (1918) – Readable & Dyslexia-Friendly Version

**Spring 1918: German Offensive Begins**  
German troops started a new offensive in March 1918. They attacked British forces quickly. Poor weather and fog caused confusion. The British may have retreated farther than needed. Germany moved again toward Paris. They began bombing the city as they had early in the war.  

Germany made peace treaties with Russia and Romania. Both countries left the war. They gave up territory as part of the deals. By summer 1918, Germany held more land than ever before in its history.  

**Summer 1918: Allied Forces Arrive**  
After four years of war, large numbers of U.S. troops finally arrived in Europe. France and Britain welcomed this help. China and Greece also joined the war. Brazil entered in October 1917. Haiti, Cuba, and most Central American nations declared war on the Central Powers between spring 1917 and summer 1918. None sent soldiers or played a major role in battles.  

The Allies now had far more troops than the Central Powers—about three times as many. This large number made it hard for Germany and its allies to keep fighting for long.  

**Summer/Fall 1918: Allied Counterattack Begins**  
The Allies started their own offensives. They won some battles. These set up events for later in the fall.  

The last major battle was the Meuse-Argonne offensive in France. It began in September 1918. This attack had been planned for many months. Hundreds of thousands of U.S. soldiers joined British and French forces. They used infantry attacks, poison gas, tanks, and aircraft. Allied armies moved forward several miles quickly. German forces held their positions at first. But over the next month, they started losing ground steadily.  

**Late Fall 1918: Germany’s Situation Worsens**  
Food shortages caused panic and despair in Germany. Many soldiers left their units without permission (deserted). Civil unrest spread across Germany and Austria-Hungary.  

German naval commanders wanted one final battle to gain glory. They planned to sail the fleet out late October to fight the British. However, most sailors knew victory was impossible. About one thousand sailors in Kiel (a major German naval base) refused to sail. Workers there also refused orders. The refusal spread to other cities quickly.  

**November 1918: Germany Ends the War**  
In Berlin, left-wing Socialist Party politicians saw the unrest as a chance for big government change. They demanded the Kaiser step down and called for a republic. Wilhelm II abdicated on November 9, 1918. He went to live in the Netherlands until his death in 1941.  

Moderate Social Democrat leaders then took charge. They formed a temporary (provisional) government. Germany became a republic. The German military agreed to work under this civilian government.  

These leaders began formal peace talks with the Allies. They believed Germany could not win the war. Ending it through an **armistice** (a cease-fire agreement) seemed best. An armistice meant fighting would stop while negotiations continued. Germany hoped this would let them keep some gains and end the war with honor—not a full surrender, which meant admitting defeat.  

The Allies chose to ask for an armistice, not a surrender. This was important. A surrender means one side officially accepts defeat. Germany did not want that in 1918. An armistice allowed talks without forcing Germany to admit total loss.  

**Terms of the Armistice (November 11, 1918)**  
The armistice started at 11:00 a.m. on November 11, 1918. Fighting stopped exactly at that minute everywhere. German troops had to leave occupied parts of France and Belgium. They returned to Germany. *(Later leaders like Adolf Hitler used the fact that German troops were still in France/Belgium when the war ended as propaganda.)*  

Germany also gave all military equipment to the Allies, including its navy. Most ships went to Scapa Flow (in the Orkney Islands, Scotland). The next year, German crews sank their own ships there rather than hand them over intact.  

**War Casualties and Aftermath**  
Casualties were extremely high. This includes people who died, were wounded, captured, or listed as missing. Russia had over nine million casualties. France had over six million. Germany and Austria-Hungary each had over seven million. Over 8.5 million soldiers died. More than twenty-one million were wounded. Millions of civilians also died or were hurt.  

Treaty negotiations began while countries recovered from the war’s damage. Talks lasted about six months after the armistice. Germany was proven wrong in its hopes for favorable terms. Much suffering and destruction remained, but the war was finally over.

### Resistance in India and the Opium Wars: A Clear Account

**Part 1: Indian Resistance to British Rule (1857)**

Resistance to European colonialism happened in India too.  
The Indian Mutiny of 1857 is also called the Sepoy Rebellion.  
It was an attempt to end British rule.  

Before 1857, Britain did not always govern India directly.  
The British East India Company used indirect rule.  
British leaders changed their minds after successes in India.  
They decided they could govern directly.  
This made Indian elites worried.  
They saw their own power slipping away.  

Many Indians were also upset by Christian missionaries.  
Missionaries tried to convert people to Christianity.  
This offended people who wanted to keep their own traditions and religions.  

Lord Dalhousie was governor-general from 1848 to 1856.  
He created a policy called the Doctrine of Lapse.  
Here is how it worked:  
Hindu rulers without a natural heir often adopted one.  
The kingdom then passed to the adopted heir.  
Dalhousie said Britain must approve any adoption.  
If there was no heir, Britain could take over the state.  
Britain rejected adoptions and took over states starting in 1848.  
This affected mostly Hindu-ruled states.  
But it alarmed all Indian aristocracy.  
They feared British takeover of their lands and power.  

Britain also believed its own culture was best.  
This led to changes that angered many Indians.  

One change involved the Hindu practice called *sati* (also spelled *suttee*).  
In *sati*, some Hindu widows were expected to burn themselves alive on their husband’s funeral pyre.  
Britain made a law to stop this.  
The law also allowed widows to remarry.  

Britain started Western schools in India.  
These schools used English as the main language.  
Before, Persian was common for education and literature, especially under the Mughals and in Islamic empires.  
Young men from these English schools got better jobs with British business or government.  
Because more Hindus attended these schools than Muslims, Hindus gained more positions of authority.  
Muslims felt they were losing power they had held for centuries.  

Tensions grew over the Enfield Rifle in 1857.  
Soldiers had to bite the end of a cartridge before loading it.  
The grease on the cartridge came from cows or pigs.  
Cows are sacred to Hindus.  
Pigs are forbidden to Muslims.  
Indian troops were upset and suspicious.  
Some believed Britain used these greases on purpose to insult them.  

In March 1857, a sepoy named Mangal Pandey started the unrest.  
He was a devout Hindu Brahmin.  
He attacked two British officers.  
The British executed him.  
This sparked a large revolt across India.  

During the Mutiny, Indians outnumbered British troops.  
But the British were more united.  
Indians could not work together easily.  
Differences in religion, ethnicity, and region divided them.  
After battles and actions by both sides that were later called war crimes, Britain declared victory on July 8, 1859.  
They executed many rebel leaders.  
Some British officers disagreed with these executions.  

The Mutiny showed the British government the East India Company could not rule well.

Britain ruled directly until India became independent in 1947.  
This time is called the **British Raj**.  
"Raj" means "rule" in Sanskrit.  
It is also called British Paramountcy.  
This meant Britain governed through the Viceroy of India.  

**Part 2: The Opium Wars with China (1839–1860)**

Britain’s trade relationship with China led to conflict later.  
China had a positive balance of trade for many years.  
Britain wanted to change this.  
They imported opium from their territories in India into China.  

People in China had used opium as medicine and lightly for recreation for centuries.  
In the early 1800s, some began smoking dried opium, inspired by tobacco from America.  
Smoking caused a much stronger effect than chewing.  
Opium addiction became a serious problem in China.  

The Chinese government banned recreational opium use in 1729.  
But British traders kept selling it.  
Prices went up sharply.  
Other nations, like France and the United States, also started selling opium in China.  
Britain controlled most of this trade from India.  

In 1839, Chinese officials seized opium stored by British merchants in Canton.  
Britain sent military forces to China.  
They demanded penalties and protection for British traders.  
This conflict became the First Opium War.  

British forces had better weapons and organization.  
They won most battles against the Chinese army of that time.  
Britain could not conquer all of China.  
But they carried out repeated raids along the coast.  
China could not effectively defend against these raids.  

In 1842, Britain and China signed the Treaty of Nanjing.  
This treaty forced China to:  
*   Give Hong Kong to Britain.  
*   Open five ports to European traders.  
*   Give Britain favorable trade terms.  
*   Pay a large fine to Britain.  

The next year, another treaty gave British citizens in China the right to be tried in British courts.  
This made them safe from Chinese courts for certain crimes.  

After some peace, the Second Opium War started in 1856.  
Chinese soldiers seized a British ship in Chinese waters.  
The crew were Chinese sailors suspected of piracy.  
Britain demanded the ship and crew back immediately.  
They also demanded an apology.  
China refused.  
The British navy attacked the Chinese coast.  

France joined Britain.  
France wanted better trade access in China too.  
The United States and Russia did not officially join the war.  
But they gave some limited support to British and French forces.  

Like the First Opium War, the Second Opium War involved European raids on the Chinese coast.  
These attacks damaged and humiliated China.  
They did not threaten China’s existence as a nation.  

The war ended in 1860 with the Convention of Beijing.  
This treaty:  
*   Gave some territories to Russia.  
*   Expanded British-controlled Hong Kong.  
*   Stopped religious discrimination against Christians in China.  
*   Allowed almost unlimited foreign access to China.  

These treaties, and others that followed, are called "unequal treaties" by China.  
China says they were forced on them, not truly negotiated.  

Hong Kong was returned to China in 1997.

### South American Independence: Peru, Leaders, and Early Diplomacy (Dyslexia-Friendly Version)

**Part 1: Entering Peru**  
Two independence armies moved toward Peru. One came from the north. It was led by Simón Bolívar. His army left the Viceroyalty of New Granada. Another army came from the south. It was led by José de San Martín. His army left the Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata and the new Republic of Chile.  
San Martín left Chile in 1820. He took land troops and sailors on ships. A Scottish ex-naval officer, Thomas Cochrane, helped him. Cochrane had joined South America’s independence fight on his own. San Martín attacked royalist Peru by sea. He landed on Lima’s shore in September 1820.  
The highlands stayed under royalist control. But San Martín’s arrival started a coastal uprising. His forces slowly gained ground. By July 28, 1821, they held Lima. Peruvian city leaders had to declare independence then. They also accepted San Martín as Protector of Peru.

**Part 2: San Martín and Bolívar Meet**  
San Martín ruled Lima militarily and civilly. But royalist troops still controlled most of Peru’s interior. People in Lima saw San Martín’s forces as foreign invaders.  
After freeing Bogotá in 1819, Bolívar moved to Ecuador. He made little progress against royalists there. San Martín and Bolívar were rivals for leadership. They decided to meet in Guayaquil, Ecuador.  
Bolívar controlled Guayaquil’s port and naval base by 1821. In 1822, he entered Quito and declared Ecuador independent.  
In July 1822, San Martín sailed to Guayaquil. He hoped merchants there would join Lima. But Bolívar arrived first. He pushed Guayaquil supporters to unite with Colombia (Bolívar’s home region). When San Martín landed, the city’s ownership was no longer discussed.  
San Martín likely felt disappointed. He met Bolívar privately. The meeting was secret. At the end, San Martín decided to let Bolívar finish liberating South America. Soon after, San Martín left the independence struggle. He went into self-imposed exile in Europe. He never returned.

**Part 3: Bolívar’s Rule and Battles**  
Bolívar occupied Lima in 1823. In February 1824, a Peruvian congress named him dictator of Peru.  
Bolívar won a key victory against Spanish forces at the Battle of Junín in August 1824. His chief of staff, Antonio José de Sucre, defeated a larger Spanish force at Ayacucho in December 1824.  
In 1825, royalist troops in Upper Peru surrendered after Sucre’s victory. They accepted a general amnesty. Upper Peru was later renamed Bolivia, honoring *El Libertador* (Bolívar).

**Part 4: Ideas and International Relations**  
Both Bolívar and San Martín thought about all of South America. They supported close alliances between new nations. San Martín liked the British constitutional monarchy, like some Mexican conservatives did. But Bolívar rejected kings as mystical figures. He believed republics were best for stability.  
In 1822, Gran Colombia was the first Spanish American nation recognized by the United States.  

**Part 5: The Monroe Doctrine and Europe**  
The United States worried European powers might use South America’s wars to intervene in the Western Hemisphere. This could threaten U.S. security and trade.  
After Napoleon’s defeat at Waterloo (1815), Austria, Prussia, and Russia formed the Holy Alliance. Its goal: protect empires by stopping revolutions like France’s. At meetings in 1820 and 1821, they claimed the right to crush rebellions threatening monarchs. In 1820-1821, Austrian troops crushed a rebellion in Naples.  
Europe did not help Spain in 1820 when Spanish liberals forced King Fernando VII to restore the 1812 Constitution. But in 1822, the Holy Alliance agreed to let France’s Louis XVIII invade Spain. The goal: end Spanish revolution and return Fernando to his throne.  
The Holy Alliance also wanted to force Fernando VII to control his American colonies. The United States opposed this. Britain, which traded heavily with Latin America, also opposed it. Britain’s foreign minister suggested the U.S. join a joint warning to France and the Holy Alliance.  
U.S. Secretary of State John Quincy Adams thought it was better for the U.S. to state its own principles clearly, not let Britain lead. With President James Monroe’s reluctant agreement, Adams announced the **Monroe Doctrine** in 1823. It warned European nations: do not interfere with independent countries in the Western Hemisphere.  
Bolívar welcomed U.S. support. But he trusted British power more to stop Spain regaining colonies. He did not see the Monroe Doctrine as very important for South America.  
In 1824, Great Britain and the United States officially recognized Gran Colombia. Gran Colombia’s representatives got a large loan from London banks.

**Part 6: The Congress of Panama and Aftermath**  
In 1826, Bolívar called the Congress of Panama. Its goals: strengthen bonds between new Spanish American nations, plan mutual cooperation, and create a permanent alliance.  
The United States, Haiti, and Brazil did not attend.  
But the main problem was internal weakness in the new countries. The revolutions’ legacy was mixed. South America had freed itself from Spain. But colonial social hierarchies remained strong. These turned into conflict between groups: enslaved Africans, Indigenous peoples, mestizos (mixed race), pardos (mixed African and European), and White people. Provinces fought each other. After beating royalists, popular armies faced civil wars over the new order after independence.  
Creole leaders like Bolívar and San Martín were not the only post-independence leaders. Local military chiefs often became powerful. They allied with wealthy creole landowners. This kept old power structures in place.

### Natural Rights in the Enlightenment: A Clear Overview

**What are natural rights?**  
Natural rights are basic rights that belong to every human being. Examples include the right to life, freedom (liberty), and safety. People discussed these ideas a lot in the 1700s (the eighteenth century).

**Where did the idea come from?**  
The idea of natural rights is older than the Enlightenment. It exists in many ancient traditions about justice and "natural law" (rules thought to come from nature or God, not just human made laws).  
*   In ancient Persia, Zoroastrianism spoke of *asha*. This means "God’s will." It describes unchanging laws that guide the universe.  
Many older religious and philosophical groups had their own views on natural law. European Enlightenment thinkers later used these old ideas to build new political systems. This was new at the time.

**Why did Enlightenment thinkers focus on this?**  
Enlightenment thinkers valued reason and wanted to improve human life. They started designing political systems based on natural rights. They did not base power on "divine right of kings" (the idea that a king gets power from God) or strict traditional Christian social rankings.

**John Locke: An early key thinker**  
English philosopher John Locke wrote about natural rights in the late 1600s. He said all people have fundamental rights to life, liberty, and property.  
In his important book, *Two Treatises of Government*, Locke argued:  
*   All people are born free.  
*   Government should only exist with the agreement (consent) of the people. This idea is called **popular sovereignty**.  
Locke and other thinkers said all humans are naturally equal. However, in practice, they supported systems like colonialism and the Atlantic slave trade. These systems denied natural rights to most people—especially women, people of color, and others—keeping power mainly with white men. This is a serious contradiction.

**French Enlightenment thinkers: Debating rights**  
French thinkers also discussed natural rights deeply.  
*   **Voltaire** (real name François-Marie d’Arouet) strongly supported basic freedoms. He criticized the Catholic Church, aristocracy, and monarchy. He especially fought for religious tolerance, free speech, and the power of reason. He wrote about this in works like *Treatise on Tolerance*. His famous book *Candide* used sharp jokes to criticize both religion and government.  
*   **Montesquieu** focused on political liberty and how laws work. He argued that a state’s powers—making laws, carrying them out, judging disputes—should be separated. This separation helps keep government power in check. He explained this in his 1748 book *The Spirit of the Laws*.

**Jean-Jacques Rousseau: The social contract**  
Rousseau built on older ideas about the **social contract**. This concept is very old—found in ancient Greek thinkers like Plato and Socrates, and also in a Buddhist text from around 200 BCE called *The Mahāvastu*.  
The social contract idea says: People give up some natural freedom to form a community (society). In return, the government must protect everyone’s rights.  
Rousseau wrote about this in *The Social Contract*. He said:  
*   Living together means we depend on each other.  
*   Individual freedom is important, but government may need to limit some actions to protect everyone’s rights safely.  
*   A government is truly fair only if it follows the **general will**—the common good of the whole community, not just what a small elite wants.

**Thinkers who questioned natural rights**  
Not all Enlightenment philosophers agreed on natural rights. Some doubted they existed at all.  
*   **Jeremy Bentham** was an English lawyer. He followed utilitarianism: the best action is the one that creates the greatest good for the greatest number of people. Bentham believed rights only exist because a government *creates* them. Rights do not exist in nature, outside society. If a government acts unfairly, arguing against it could cause chaos, he warned.  
*   **Edmund Burke** (an Irish philosopher) also rejected popular sovereignty (government by the people’s direct consent). He accepted natural law but thought its rules become less important once civil society (organized communities) forms. Only wise and virtuous leaders should hold power, serving the state’s best interests. Ordinary people, he believed, should set aside selfish desires for the good of the whole society.

**What did the Enlightenment achieve?**  
Even with many different views, the Enlightenment changed how people thought about government and rights.  
*   It helped people question their relationship with authority.  
*   It made more people think seriously about when revolution (overthrowing a government) might be justified.  
*   While some thinkers (like Burke and Bentham) prioritized state order over individual rights, others (like Locke and Voltaire) strongly defended natural rights and political freedom.  
*   The debates about natural rights led to deeper discussions about social contract theory, law ethics, and how fair political systems should be built. These conversations continue today.

### Natural Rights in the Enlightenment: A Clear Overview

**What are natural rights?**  
Natural rights are basic rights that belong to every human being. Examples include the right to life, freedom (liberty), and safety. People discussed these ideas a lot in the 1700s (the eighteenth century).

**Where did the idea come from?**  
The idea of natural rights is older than the Enlightenment. It exists in many ancient traditions about justice and "natural law" (rules thought to come from nature or God, not just human made laws).  
In ancient Persia, Zoroastrianism spoke of *asha*. This means "God’s will." It describes unchanging laws that guide the universe.  
Many older religious and philosophical groups had their own views on natural law. European Enlightenment thinkers later used these old ideas to build new political systems. This was new at the time.

**Why did Enlightenment thinkers focus on this?**  
Enlightenment thinkers valued reason and wanted to improve human life. They started designing political systems based on natural rights. They did not base power on "divine right of kings" (the idea that a king gets power from God) or strict traditional Christian social rankings.

**John Locke: An early key thinker**  
English philosopher John Locke wrote about natural rights in the late 1600s. He said all people have fundamental rights to life, liberty, and property.  
In his important book, *Two Treatises of Government*, Locke argued:  
*   All people are born free.  
*   Government should only exist with the agreement (consent) of the people. This idea is called **popular sovereignty**.  
Locke and other thinkers said all humans are naturally equal. However, in practice, they supported systems like colonialism and the Atlantic slave trade. These systems denied natural rights to most people—especially women, people of color, and others—keeping power mainly with white men. This is a serious contradiction.

**French Enlightenment thinkers: Debating rights**  
French thinkers also discussed natural rights deeply.  
*   **Voltaire** (real name François-Marie d’Arouet) strongly supported basic freedoms. He criticized the Catholic Church, aristocracy, and monarchy. He especially fought for religious tolerance, free speech, and the power of reason. He wrote about this in works like *Treatise on Tolerance*. His famous book *Candide* used sharp jokes to criticize both religion and government.  
*   **Montesquieu** focused on political liberty and how laws work. He argued that a state’s powers—making laws, carrying them out, judging disputes—should be separated. This separation helps keep government power in check. He explained this in his 1748 book *The Spirit of the Laws*.

**Jean-Jacques Rousseau: The social contract**  
Rousseau built on older ideas about the **social contract**. This concept is very old—found in ancient Greek thinkers like Plato and Socrates, and also in a Buddhist text from around 200 BCE called *The Mahāvastu*.  
The social contract idea says: People give up some natural freedom to form a community (society). In return, the government must protect everyone’s rights.  
Rousseau wrote about this in *The Social Contract*. He said:  
*   Living together means we depend on each other.  
*   Individual freedom is important, but government may need to limit some actions to protect everyone’s rights safely.  
*   A government is truly fair only if it follows the **general will**—the common good of the whole community, not just what a small elite wants.

**Thinkers who questioned natural rights**  
Not all Enlightenment philosophers agreed on natural rights. Some doubted they existed at all.  
*   **Jeremy Bentham** was an English lawyer. He followed utilitarianism: the best action is the one that creates the greatest good for the greatest number of people. Bentham believed rights only exist because a government *creates* them. Rights do not exist in nature, outside society. If a government acts unfairly, arguing against it could cause chaos, he warned.  
*   **Edmund Burke** (an Irish philosopher) also rejected popular sovereignty (government by the people’s direct consent). He accepted natural law but thought its rules become less important once civil society (organized communities) forms. Only wise and virtuous leaders should hold power, serving the state’s best interests. Ordinary people, he believed, should set aside selfish desires for the good of the whole society.

**What did the Enlightenment achieve?**  
Even with many different views, the Enlightenment changed how people thought about government and rights.  
*   It helped people question their relationship with authority.  
*   It made more people think seriously about when revolution (overthrowing a government) might be justified.  
*   While some thinkers (like Burke and Bentham) prioritized state order over individual rights, others (like Locke and Voltaire) strongly defended natural rights and political freedom.  
*   The debates about natural rights led to deeper discussions about social contract theory, law ethics, and how fair political systems should be built. These conversations continue today.

**Stalin’s Economic Plans and Collectivization: A Clear Account**

Stalin set economic goals in documents called Five-Year Plans. Each plan listed what the Soviet Union should achieve by its end. The plans were very ambitious. Meeting the goals was hard. Officials risked losing their jobs or even their lives if they failed to meet production targets.

The first Five-Year Plan focused on rapid industrialization. Stalin dropped his earlier support for slow growth. He wanted more farm equipment for peasants. He also wanted to show he could push industry faster than his critics. New cities were built around specific industries. Iron and steel production needed to rise sharply. New power stations had to be constructed. Many goals were met. Overall industrial capacity grew by about 50 percent.

Stalin’s plan for total state control faced big problems in agriculture. This was called collectivization. Collectivization meant moving from small private farms to large state-run collective farms. Party officials pushed hard to meet higher grain quotas after the first plan ended. They often ignored how farming actually worked. Peasants strongly resisted government interference in their daily work. Resistance sometimes turned violent. The revolution had promised peasants better lives. They saw collectivization as destroying that promise.

The government targeted a group called *kulaks*. Kulaks were farmers who had prospered under the earlier NEP (New Economic Policy). In the early 1920s, the Soviet government defined a kulak as owning a farm of 25 to 40 acres and hiring seasonal workers. Few farmers fit this exact size. But Stalin blamed kulaks for collectivization problems. He called them enemies of the state. Kulaks could be arrested or executed. Their family members also suffered. They were blocked from certain jobs or university studies.

Stalin pushed collectivization faster. Local officials worked hard to hit new grain targets. By 1939, over 90 percent of peasants lived and worked on collective farms. Peasants who resisted could be arrested. Many were sent to labor camps in Siberia. Poor peasants often joined the system because they had little to lose. Middle-class peasants usually opposed it strongly. Some killed their own livestock rather than give animals to the state. Over half the country’s livestock died during collectivization in the 1930s. Numbers did not fully recover until the 1950s. In some places, spring planting was missed due to chaos.

Collectivization caused millions of deaths. About two million people died while resisting or in prison. Between five and ten million more died in a famine. The famine came from collectivization chaos, peasants slaughtering livestock, and government taking food. Ukraine’s grain region suffered terribly. Government actions there caused mass starvation. Officials sometimes entered homes to take all available food. About 3.9 million Ukrainians died in this famine. They called it the Holodomor, meaning "death by famine" in Ukrainian.

Collectivization problems made many Party members doubt Stalin’s choices. In 1934, a high-ranking politician named Sergei Kirov was assassinated. Stalin believed this murder revealed a plot against him. Kirov’s death, plus the unrest from collectivization, Nazi Germany’s rise (1933), and knowing some Party members disagreed with him—all fed Stalin’s growing fear. He felt surrounded by enemies. This led to a reign of terror. The secret police arrested millions suspected of disloyalty. Many were sent to Siberian prison camps. They often died from hunger or overwork. Some were executed after very short trials. Others received no trial at all.

The victims of the 1930s purges included many groups: kulaks, former tsarist officials, intellectuals, Russian Orthodox priests, ethnic minorities, workers labeled "saboteurs" after factory accidents (during the rushed Five-Year Plan work), Red Army officers, government officials, prominent Soviet politicians, and early supporters of Lenin. Historians disagree on the exact number killed in these purges. One million is a widely accepted estimate.

### Women’s Rights and Social Change After World War I

The war ended in 1918. The fight for women’s right to vote had been going on for many decades in the United States and Britain. People who supported this cause were called suffragists. Some suffragists took very bold actions to get attention. For example, Emily Davison stepped in front of the King of England’s horse at a race in 1913. She was killed. Suffragist leaders in both countries were often arrested. Many went on hunger strikes while in jail. Guards forced them to eat. This drew more attention to their cause.

Women had supported the war strongly. They worked in war industries and in medical corps units. This hard work made politicians more willing to consider women voting. In the United States, women won the right to vote in 1920. The law stated this was because of their war service. Britain changed its voting rules in steps. In 1918, women over thirty who owned property could vote. In 1928, all women aged twenty-one and older could vote. That same year, men also gained easier voting rules. Property requirements for men ended in 1918. All men twenty-one and older could then vote. For soldiers, the age limit was nineteen.

Other countries followed these changes. German women got the right to vote in 1918. The new country of Poland gave all women the vote immediately after its creation. Some other countries still had limits. They required property ownership or being a war widow to vote. France and Italy were slower. Women could not vote in either country until 1945. In Japan, groups of women argued for political roles through the 1920s and 1930s. Japanese law allowed women to attend political meetings. But women did not get the right to vote until after World War II. Rising feminism in China, linked to the May Fourth Movement, helped women gain legal rights to own property themselves.

Individual women also spoke out clearly. Huda Sha’arawi founded the Egyptian Feminist Union in 1923. She stopped wearing her veil and headscarf. She had already started schools for girls. She was active in Egypt’s independence movement too. Later, she became vice president of the International Women’s Union in the 1930s. Zaynab al-Ghazali founded the Muslim Women’s Society in Europe in 1936. Al-Ghazali said women could take part in politics outside the home and still follow Islam.

Several minority groups in the United States hoped military service would bring them more rights and acceptance. More than eleven thousand Native Americans served in the military during the war. Many believed this service would earn them U.S. citizenship. In 1924, Native Americans were granted U.S. citizenship. African Americans also saw the war as a chance to prove their loyalty. They had faced discriminatory laws and racial segregation for a long time. The U.S. military was segregated. Black units overseas, especially in France, saw different treatment. There, they could move more freely and were often treated with respect. Black soldiers in France sometimes served in combat roles. In the U.S., most Black service members were kept in support jobs. Many felt hopeful that life in the United States would improve after the war.

After 1918, however, little had changed for many people. Discriminatory laws stayed in place. Poor treatment of veterans, including Black and Native American veterans, was common. What *was* new was greater possibility for movement. In 1917, good-paying jobs in war factories began drawing African American workers northward. This continued after the war as factories made consumer goods. By 1920, over one million African Americans had left the rural South. This movement was called the Great Migration. It continued for many decades.

Racism existed strongly in the North too. In the summer of 1919, race riots happened in many cities. In the 1920s, the Ku Klux Klan, a white supremacist group formed after the Civil War, spread across the nation. Northern racism seemed less severe than what African Americans had experienced in the South. Still, northern cities offered more job and education opportunities. This drew many people to northern and midwestern cities. New jobs and groups like the NAACP helped build the New Negro movement in the 1920s. This movement aimed to rebuild racial pride, express culture freely, gain economic independence, and support fair politics. One early goal was a federal law against lynching. Lynching was a vigilante crime. Its victims were almost always African Americans. Southern state courts rarely punished white men who committed these murders. Activists wanted lynching made a federal crime, so it could be tried in federal court. They hoped this would bring more justice. An anti-lynching bill was introduced in Congress in 1922 and again in 1935. Southern white politicians blocked both votes. They opposed any federal action, even for humanitarian reasons.

Racial pride also shaped the Harlem Renaissance. This was a burst of African American literature, art, and music named after a neighborhood in New York City where many people from the Great Migration settled. The Harlem Renaissance flourished in the 1920s. It brought the work of many Black writers into mainstream view. Poet Langston Hughes and writer Zora Neale Hurston were key figures. Hurston wrote novels, short stories, and plays about African American struggles in the twentieth century. Music in Harlem and other Black communities featured blues and jazz. These styles became international genres. They also provided the soundtrack for the big changes after World War I.

The Harlem Renaissance, especially the poems of Jamaican-born Claude McKay, inspired a movement called Négritude. This literary movement began in French-speaking parts of Africa and the Americas. It was founded by Léopold Sédar Senghor, a Senegalese poet and professor. Aimé Césaire, a poet from the Caribbean island of Martinique (then a French colony), coined the term Négritude. The movement called on Black people to reject European culture and values. It urged them to embrace African cultures instead.

**World War II Scientific Developments (Dyslexia-Accessible Version)**

World War II caused many scientific and technological changes. These changes became matters of life and death. The war itself changed how governments worked with scientists. Governments spent money on weapons and other technologies needed for the war and for national security.

In fall 1939, British scientists quickly changed their work. They moved from pure research to helping the war effort.

Advances in radio waves led to radar. Radar gave early warning of enemy attacks. Other advances added electronics like microwaves and early computers to military use. This helped spread electronics into everyday life after the war.

Allied efforts to break Nazi spy codes started the first simple computers. British mathematician Alan Turing and his team worked for the British Secret Service. They tried to break the Nazi Enigma code, which seemed unbreakable. To do this, they built a device. This device tested hundreds of thousands of possible code keys in intercepted messages. They succeeded in breaking the code.

Another computing breakthrough was ENIAC. ENIAC stood for Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer. The U.S. Army first used it to calculate artillery shots. It calculated much faster than earlier machines, using electricity instead of moving parts. By 1955, ENIAC had done more calculations than all humans combined up to that point.

Medical science also advanced during the war. A key medical development was penicillin. Scientists improved how to make and use penicillin. This allowed mass production of the antibiotic.

Charles Drew, an African American doctor, made another life-saving advance. He developed a better way to store blood plasma. Plasma could be kept longer than whole blood. It also worked well as a replacement for whole-blood transfusions in emergencies.

However, racial bias appeared in 1941. The U.S. Red Cross followed a War Department rule. They labeled blood and plasma as either "White" or "Negro." Dr. Drew resigned from the National Blood Bank because this policy was racist and unscientific.

The biggest scientific effort was building the atomic bomb. In December 1938, German physicists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split atoms. This discovery was called nuclear fission. A few months later, Germany started a secret program, the Uranium Club, to build an atomic bomb.

German-born physicist Albert Einstein had recently moved to the U.S. He knew the danger of Nazi research. With help from physicist Leo Szilard, Einstein wrote a letter to President Roosevelt. The letter warned about Nazi work and urged the U.S. to start its own program.

By the late 1930s, British scientists and others believed an atomic bomb was possible. Teams of physicists, including refugees from Nazi Germany, began experiments. They studied nuclear chain reactions, which cause atomic explosions.

In August 1942, the U.S. government started the top-secret Manhattan Project. Workers at many sites across the U.S. began building the first atomic bomb. Sites included Los Alamos in New Mexico, Oak Ridge in Tennessee, and Hanford in Washington State. About 600,000 people worked on this urgent project.

Germany and Japan also tried to build atomic bombs. Germany faced problems. Many top German scientists had left Germany. Some even helped the Manhattan Project. Also, Hitler preferred funding V2 bombers for attacks on England over an atomic bomb.

Japan started its own project in 1941. Physicist Yoshio Nishina led it, called Ni-Go. Japan learned little from Germany due to U.S. air raids and lack of shared information. Progress on the Japanese atomic bomb was slow.

In July 1945, the Manhattan Project succeeded. Scientists detonated a test bomb at Trinity in New Mexico. William L. Laurence, the project historian, described this moment: "On that moment hung eternity. Time stood still. Space contracted to a pinpoint. It was as though the earth had opened and the skies split. One felt as though they had been privileged to witness the Birth of the World—to be present at the moment of Creation when the Lord Said: Let there be light."

President Roosevelt died suddenly in April 1945. Vice President Harry S. Truman became president. Truman then had to decide whether to use the new atomic weapon.

**Cold War Beginnings: Clear and Accessible Version**

*   The United States and the Soviet Union both saw themselves as the main leader of the world after World War II.
*   They had worked together to defeat Hitler. But their deep differences returned quickly.
*   The United States wanted a world with democratically governed nations. These countries should live peacefully and be prosperous through capitalism.
*   The Soviet Union wanted communism to lead all countries to peace and prosperity. It also wanted to never fear invasion from the west again.
*   This goal was why Stalin set up **satellite states** in Eastern Europe. These were countries under Soviet control. Stalin put pro-Soviet, communist governments in power there.
*   In 1944, at the Moscow Conference, U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt did not attend. British Prime Minister Winston Churchill agreed: Stalin could install communist parties to control Romania and Bulgaria. These had been German allies in the war.
*   In return, Stalin promised Britain would control the Balkans (southern Europe).
*   By summer 1945, at the Potsdam Conference, things had changed. Churchill no longer wanted Stalin to have so much power in Eastern Europe. He warned new U.S. President Harry Truman about this danger. Truman did not know what was agreed at Moscow.
*   But Stalin then put a pro-Soviet government in power in Poland. This tightened Soviet control over the region.
*   In March 1946, Churchill gave a speech in Fulton, Missouri. He said an "iron curtain" now cut Europe in two. Half the continent was under Soviet domination.
*   This split of the world into U.S.-allied and Soviet-allied parts defined the **Cold War**. The Cold War lasted until the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
*   It was called "cold" because there was no direct fighting between U.S. and Soviet military forces. (A "hot" war has actual armed conflict between countries.)
*   Europe split further in 1948. Czechoslovakia had a government with both communists and non-communists. Stalin’s forces replaced it with an all-communist government loyal to Moscow.
*   In 1949, Hungary also came under control of a communist party allied with the Soviet Union.
*   The main U.S. strategy in the Cold War was **containment**. This meant trying to stop Soviet influence from spreading beyond Eastern Europe.
*   The idea of containment first came from George F. Kennan. He was a U.S. diplomat in Moscow. In his Long Telegram to the State Department, he wrote:
    *   The Soviet government seemed paranoid and aimed to fight capitalism.
    *   Soviet leaders could not be moved by reason; they only understood force.
    *   Therefore, attempts to spread communism must meet strong resistance.
*   The Soviet Union’s foreign goals after World War II were opposite the U.S. goals.

**Trenches on the Western Front**

The stalemate in late 1914 led to trenches. Both sides dug them deep for protection. These trenches became the main fighting area of World War I.

Constant artillery fire and deep mud made trench life hard. Soldiers dug down to hide from enemy shells. They often stayed in one spot for days.

German troops dug deeper, stronger trenches early on. They expected to stay there a long time. Allied trenches started simple but improved over the years.

At their longest, trenches stretched about 500 miles across France and Belgium.  
Front-line soldiers spent days in the front trench. Then they moved back to support trenches, then reserve trenches.  
Behind the reserves were artillery positions.  
Further back were field hospitals and villages.

Life in the trenches was hard and boring. Death was always close, just above the trench edge. It rained often. Trenches filled with thick mud. Soldiers laid wooden planks on the ground to help. But feet and legs stayed wet. This caused a condition called trench foot. Skin would rot, split, and peel off. It was very painful and hard to prevent.  
Trenches also collected trash and debris. Disease spread easily in the close, dirty space.

Sometimes, soldiers from both sides spoke across no-man’s land. An example happened in December 1914, the first Christmas of the war. German and British soldiers called out to each other. First one side sang carols, then the other. Slowly, some climbed out of their trenches. They met in the middle ground between them. There, they shared cigarettes, candy, and small souvenirs. Many soldiers wrote about similar moments. This Christmas truce showed human kindness during war. But leaders at headquarters did not allow it to happen again.

Other battles were not always in trenches.  
Italian and Austro-Hungarian troops fought in the high Alps mountains. Soldiers faced thin air, little food, and deep snow. Frostbite and avalanches were real dangers. More than half the casualties here came from cold and snow, not just bullets. Narrow mountain passes also made retreat hard.

Fighting began in 1914 between Russians and Ottomans in the Caucasus. The area was isolated. Ottoman forces lacked good roads to bring supplies far from the front. Deep snow and temperatures below freezing made travel hard. Without enough food and supplies, Ottoman troops suffered many casualties—tens of thousands.

In dry places like the Mediterranean and Middle East, armies needed water. Finding enough water for people and animals was difficult. Horses needed feed, which was scarce. In the Middle East especially, soldiers used camels more to carry supplies and people. Camels handled the desert heat better than horses.

chapter_key: Life in the Trenches, the Mountains, and the Desert
text:
Trenches were built on the Western Front.  
The stalemate in late 1914 led to trenches.  
Both sides dug them deep for protection.  
These trenches became the main fighting area of World War One.  
Constant artillery fire made trench life hard.  
Deep mud added to the difficulty.  
Soldiers dug down to hide from enemy shells.  
They often stayed in one spot for days.  
German troops dug deeper stronger trenches early on.  
They expected to stay there a long time.  
Allied trenches started simple but improved over the years.  
At their longest, trenches stretched about 500 miles across France and Belgium.  
Front line soldiers spent days in the front trench.  
Then they moved back to support trenches.  
Then reserve trenches.  
Behind reserves were artillery positions.  
Further back were field hospitals.  
Villages were even further back.  
Life in the trenches was hard and boring.  
Death was always close just above the trench edge.  
It rained often.  
Trenches filled with thick mud.  
Soldiers laid wooden planks on the ground to help.  
But feet and legs stayed wet.  
This caused a condition called trench foot.  
Skin would rot, split, and peel off.  
It was very painful and hard to prevent.  
Trenches also collected trash and debris.  
Disease spread easily in close dirty space.  
Sometimes soldiers from both sides spoke across no-man's land.  
An example happened in December 1914, the first Christmas of the war.  
German and British soldiers called out to each other.  
First one side sang carols.  
Then the other side sang too.  
Slowly some climbed out of their trenches.  
They met in the middle ground between them.  
There they shared cigarettes, candy, and small souvenirs.  
Many soldiers wrote about similar moments.  
This Christmas truce showed human kindness during war.  
But leaders at headquarters did not allow it to happen again.  
Other battles were not always in trenches.  
Italian and Austro Hungarian troops fought in the high Alps mountains.  
Soldiers faced thin air, little food, and deep snow.  
Frostbite and avalanches were real dangers.  
More than half the casualties here came from cold and snow, not just bullets.  
Narrow mountain passes also made retreat hard.  
Fighting began in 1914 between Russians and Ottomans in the Caucasus.  
The area was isolated.  
Ottoman forces lacked good roads to bring supplies far from the front.  
Deep snow and temperatures below freezing made travel hard.  
Without enough food and supplies, Ottoman troops suffered many casualties, tens of thousands.  
In dry places like the Mediterranean and Middle East, armies needed water.  
Finding enough water for people and animals was difficult.  
Horses needed feed which was scarce.  
In the Middle East especially, soldiers used camels more to carry supplies and people.  
Camels handled the desert heat better than horses.

### Soil, Water, and Drought in West Africa  
*(Revised for readability and dyslexia access)*  

**Soil erosion is not a widespread problem across West Africa under traditional farming.**  
But it *is* a common issue in some places. It can become serious with new farming methods.  
Soil erosion links closely to water problems and desert growth. We discuss both topics together here.  

**Water supply in tropical Africa is often low.**  
Rainfall is usually less than what crops need for healthy growth.  
Rain also comes irregularly: amounts vary, and seasons are unpredictable.  
When rain does fall, it is often very heavy and fast.  
This means farmers must use every drop wisely. They must also protect land from quick floods after heavy rain.  

*Note: A separate section covers the Sahel drought in detail.*  

**Covering soil with plants or mulch helps conserve water.**  
But keeping wild plants just for cover wastes moisture that crops could use.  
This only works where there is enough water for both plants and crops.  
Using dead plant material (like straw or leaves) as mulch is usually not practical.  
Farmers need these materials for other important uses (feed, fuel, building).  
Artificial mulches (like bitumen mixed with water) are possible in theory.  
But they are rarely affordable or suitable given current resources and farming systems.  

**Building contours and tie-ridges on slopes saves water well.**  
They slow down rainwater flowing off the land.  
Using both methods together works very effectively.  
These techniques offer simple, good ways to manage water and stop soil erosion.  
But soil type must still be considered for best results.  

*Important:* These measures need large rehabilitation projects.  
Projects include engineering work, tree planting, changes to traditional farming, and sometimes changing where people live or how land is shared.  
This needs significant money and expert help.  
These costs are high. They could be used for direct farm improvements instead of fixing past problems.  

**Rainfall in West Africa is often inconsistent. Long droughts are major problems.**  
The Sahel region has a history of severe drought.  
But most West African countries face environmental challenges too.  
For about 30 years, unreliable rain and high variability have hurt farming.  

**Good rains keep soil moist and well-aerated. This supports strong crop growth.**  
In rice farming (e.g., Sierra Leone, Gambia), poor rain causes production swings.  

**Drought is the worst climatic problem for West African agriculture since the 1960s.**  
The worst periods were the 1970s and early 1980s.  
Drought changed what crops farmers grew.  
It sharply reduced yields of many traditional crops: sorghum, millet, and rice.  

*Example: Gambia*  
- Farmers say drought has worsened rain patterns.  
- Rain is the main water source for crops here.  
- Good rains in the 1950s–60s increased farm output.  
- Late 1960s/early 1970s saw rainfall decline.  
  *Example: June rains in the 1970s were much lower and shorter than in the 1950s.*  
- Rice is a major staple food in Gambia, Sierra Leone, and Sahelian states.  
  About 20–30% of Gambian land is used for upland rice.  
  Women mainly grow this rice; it is a key income source.  
- Since drought began, rice production dropped by about half.  
- Many people now rely on imported rice.  
- Less rain reduced water flowing onto rice fields (runoff).  
- Rivers have also dried up due to less rain.  

**Other main crops hurt by drought: millet, sorghum, groundnuts.**  
Farmers choose where to plant based on natural rain.  
With drought, men often move to areas with better soil moisture.  
This increases land damage (degradation) in places like Burkina Faso, Mali, and Gambia.  
It also leads to more water pollution near rivers as people settle closer to water sources.  

**Poor, erratic rain since 1968 lowered yields of these crops across countries.**  
Seed germination has also reduced, especially for millet and sorghum seeds.  

**Ghana is very vulnerable to climate change and changing weather.**  
About 35% of Ghana’s land is desert or becoming desert.  
Since the 1980s, desert growth (desertification) in northern Ghana has increased.  
It is currently destroying about 20,000 hectares of land each year.  
This threatens water resources.  

**In northern Ghana, farmers grow staple grains:** maize, rice, millet, sorghum, soybean, cowpea, groundnut.  
They also raise small livestock like sheep and goats.

### A History of Islam in West Africa: The Jakhanke Movement (Dyslexia-Accessible Version)

A history of Islam in West Africa must include the Jakhanke Islamic Movement. It began in the 12th century. Its founder was Alhajj Salim Suwareh, a respected scholar. He helped spread Islam in present-day Mali, Guinea, Senegal, and The Gambia. These four countries are among the most Islamized in West Africa today.

his work was key to its success.  
details of his early life are unclear.  
but some facts are known:  
he died around 1500 ce.  
he made seven pilgrimages to mecca.  
he had relatives there.  
he may have lived there before moving to west africa to spread islam.  
after his seventh pilgrimage he stayed in africa.  
he led his group from the jaka region of masina (in present-day mali) to jaka bambuku.  
when the ruler of bambuku became hostile—he followed traditional religion—suwareh and his students left.  
they moved towards present-day senegambia.  
this was like prophet muhammad’s migration when meccans opposed him (the hijra).  
historian professor sanneh notes since this journey jakhanke have been united by strong loyalty to suwareh’s peaceful way of teaching islam.  

how did they stay true to peace?  
the jakhanke were strict about using only peaceful methods.  
for example:  
in 1835-1887 a serahuli religious leader named momodou lamin drammeh wanted to wage war.  
he wanted to force bundu (in eastern senegal) into islam.  
the main jakhanke community rejected him and his violent approach.  
they moved further south into present-day eastern gambia.  
drammeh’s aggressive style was the opposite of jakhanke’s orderly teaching based methods.  
other leaders like umar taal or maba jahou bah also used force.  
but jakhanke did not.  
without using swords they steadily spread and strengthened islam through community education.  

a note on their approach:  
it might seem surprising.  
suwareh had family in mecca.  
why did the jakhanke reject strict uncompromising views like wahhabism?  
why did they follow a path of accommodation instead?  
this means working with local communities peacefully.  
this peaceful choice was central to their identity from the start.  

why does this matter today?  
in short: the jakhanke movement shows how islam spread successfully through peaceful community led teaching.  
they focused on education.  
they built trust.  
they lived out islamic values in daily life.  
their example starting over 500 years ago had a deep lasting impact.  
it showed west african societies that islam could be a way of peace within their own communities.  
people today who use violence to spread religion should consider this historical example.  
the jakhanke path—teaching building schools and living peacefully—offered a different enduring model for bringing islam to new areas.

Portuguese sailors first reached sub-Saharan Africa in 1442.  
They sailed to the Senegal river.  

Before this, Portuguese ships had been sailing along Morocco and Western Sahara since 1413.  
In 1413, they captured the city of Ceuta.  
Ceuta is still a Spanish city today.  

Between 1413 and the 1440s, the Portuguese built several fortified settlements on the Moroccan coast.  
Key places were: Arzila, Mogador (now called Essaouira), Safi, and Tangier.  
Portuguese presence in Morocco was strong until 1578.

Early main trade and settlement sites were:  
*   The Gambia river  
*   Bugendo on the São Domingos river in Guinea-Bissau  
*   Sierra Leone

English and French traders also had smaller missions.

### Portuguese Exploration in West Africa (1442–1510s)

Portuguese ships reached the Senegal River in 1442.  
Their voyages continued after this.  

By 1448, some sailors sailed up the Gambia River.  
They reached Kantora, a major trading town.  
Kantora is near today’s Basse Santa Su, in eastern Senegal.  
At that time, Kantora was important for trans-Saharan trade.  

In the mid-1450s, trade began with the Wolof state of Kajoor on the coast.  
The Bijagós Islands (off Guinea-Bissau) also started talks with European traders.  

Arabic was likely the first main language between people.  
Many Portuguese knew Arabic in the 1500s.  
Granada in Spain was still an Islamic kingdom then.  
Arabic was also widely spoken across West Africa.  

In 1456, one sailor wrote about the Bijagós.  
He said this was the last place where Africans shared a language with Portuguese sailors.  
This suggests Arabic and trans-Saharan trade probably did not go further south at that time.  

Portuguese ships likely reached the Cape Verde Islands around 1456.  
Historians discuss whether people lived there before this.  
Archaeology does not give clear answers.  
Some think the islands were a salt depot for Saharan states.  

Around 1471, Portuguese explored the Ghana coastline.  
This area was close to Akan forest gold mines.  
Akan traders began selling gold quietly to Portuguese ships.  
The Portuguese government wanted its share of this trade.  

In 1481, a large Portuguese fleet arrived at Edina (now called Elmina).  
They negotiated with Kwamena Ansa, the ruler there.  
The goal was to build a fortress.  
Tensions were high during talks.  
This happened because the Portuguese first tried to build the fort near a sacred site.  
After talks ended, the fortress at Elmina was built.  
It still stands today on what became known as the Gold Coast.  
Later, in the 1600s, the Dutch took over this fortress.  
By then, the Dutch and English were the main European traders in Ghana.  

Because trade grew so much on the Gold Coast, many Akan rulers wanted more trading links.  
The Portuguese built forts at other places along the coast, such as Axim and Komenda.  
Most of these forts were finished by 1500.  
Over time, forts were built almost every few miles along the Gold Coast.  
Some forts traded only gold.  
Others, like Anishan, exported corn, which European ships also needed.  
The slave trade did not become the main trade on the Gold Coast until the 1700s.  

Other West and West-Central African rulers also met Portuguese sailors.  
Oba Ozolua of Benin welcomed Portuguese visitors in 1485.  
An Atlantic trading post, Gwatón, was founded around 1490.  
Benin first sold malaguetta peppers to the Portuguese.  
But after a sea route to India opened in 1499, Europe bought fewer peppers.  
The Portuguese tried to send enslaved people from Benin to Elmina’s gold traders.  
Oba Ozolua refused this request.  

Over the 1500s, Benin’s contact with Portugal slowly decreased.  
By the early 1600s, Benin Obas made new links with Dutch traders.  
Dutch wanted Benin’s cloth.  
Through the 1600s, cloth remained Benin’s main export.  
Special embassy cloths were traded regularly to Elmina and even as far as Brazil.  
But demand for Benin cloth fell in the late 1600s.  
This happened because luxury cloths from India became more popular.  
By the 1700s, Benin Obas had to rely on the trade of enslaved persons.  
They did this to keep and rebuild power in Edo and the Benin state.  

Portuguese ships kept sailing south after Benin.  
They reached the mouth of the Kongo River.  
They made contact with Nzika Nkuwu, the manikongo (king) at Mbanza Kongo, the capital.  
The island of São Tomé was settled by 1485.  
Many BaKongo people were taken there as enslaved persons to work on sugar plantations.  

In 1491, Nzika Nkuwu converted to Christianity.  
He took the name João I.  
This led to stronger connections between Kongo, Elmina, and São Tomé.  
By the 1510s, traders from Benin were active at the Kongolese port of Mpinda.  
A Portuguese letter from the new manikongo, Afonso I (who ruled 1509–1546), mentions this.  

Therefore, by the 1510s, many different West and West-Central African peoples and rulers had contact with the Portuguese.  
Some, like Benin and Elmina, also linked to Kongo.  
African rulers often wanted more trading contacts.  
At times, they sought military support against rivals.  
This happened in Benin (against Nupe in 1516) and during civil wars in Jolof and Kongo.

Missionaries improved health services in many ways.  
Before missionaries arrived, most sick people used herbal medicines.

Roman Catholics introduced organised medical services early.  
Father Jean Marie Coquard worked in Abeokuta for 40 years.

**Revised Chapter: WWII's Impact on West Africa**

World War II speeded up nationalism. It also weakened imperialism.  
The war had a huge effect on West Africa’s economy.  

1.  West Africa became more important to the world market.  
    Europe needed more rubber, cotton, cocoa, palm oil, and groundnuts from tropical Africa.  
    Colonial governments asked colonies to grow more of these crops for sale.  
    In Nigeria, export values rose sharply.  
    *   Exports: £10,300,000 in 1931 → £24,600,000 in 1946.  
    *   Imports: £6,800,000 in 1931 → £19,800,000 in 1946.  

2.  Workers and businessmen had reasons to complain.  
    Governments set crop prices. They controlled how crops were sold. They limited wages. They pushed for higher production.  
    African traders could not join import or export trade. Only European firms were allowed.  

3.  Trade unions grew stronger.  
    The cost of living went up, but wages did not rise as fast.  
    This encouraged workers to organize.  
    In Nigeria, the number of trade unions increased from 5 to 70.  
    The Nigerian Trade Union Congress (formed in 1943) became the main group linking unions.  
    Unions worked closely with nationalist leaders for an end to colonial rule.  

4.  Cities grew quickly during and after the war.  
    Many people moved to cities for jobs.  
    Some West African cities more than doubled in size.  
    *   Lagos: 100,000 people in 1939 → 230,000 in 1950.  
    *   Accra: 70,000 people in 1941 → 166,000 in 1948.  
    Towns became crowded. Many job-seekers and workers saw Europeans living in comfortable areas with paved streets and gardens. They lived in poor slums themselves.  
    This made people more open to nationalist ideas. They later became early members of militant nationalist groups.  

5.  War encouraged education.  
    The economic boom during the war meant many families could afford school fees.  
    More people learned to read. Newspaper readership grew.  
    Nationalists used newspapers to call for political, economic, and social change.  

6.  Despite more jobs, many young people stayed unemployed.  
    Cities now had a new group of unemployed people.  
    They were angry. They blamed the colonial government and European firms.  
    They were easy to persuade by nationalist activists.  

7.  The strongest reason for growing nationalism was the return of ex-servicemen.  
    Over 176,000 men from British West Africa served in the colonial army during the war.  
    After the war, many returned home.  
    *   About 100,000 returned to Nigeria.  
    *   About 65,000 returned to Ghana (from the Middle East, East Africa, Burma, and India).  
    Soldiers had seen life in other countries. They lived well in the army.  
    They saw strong nationalist movements in Asia.  
    They fought alongside Europeans and saw their weaknesses. This broke the idea of European racial superiority.  
    Ex-servicemen came home wanting a better life for themselves and all Africans. They demanded freedom, as they had fought and died for it elsewhere.  
    Many joined militant nationalist groups.
