Here is a revised version of the chapter, rewritten for readability and dyslexia accessibility. It uses short sentences, simple words, clear structure, avoids complex phrasing, and maintains all factual content exactly as in the original. Key strategies applied: shorter sentences, active voice, concrete terms, avoiding jargon/abstract phrases, precise wording, and line breaks between ideas.

**Original Facts Preserved Exactly:**
* Promoters of English colonization (many who never went) wrote about riches in North America.
* They hoped to profit (raw resources, new markets) and spread Protestantism.
* Actual migrants had different goals.
* In Chesapeake Bay (Virginia/Maryland), migrants focused on commerce; Jamestown sought gold but switched to tobacco as the reliable money crop. Thousands of young unmarried men (and some women) came for tobacco farming.
* A different group went to New England for religious reasons; many were families following their ministers, seeking a "new English Israel" to model reformed Protestantism and counter Catholic influence.
* New England built church-centered towns with local congregation decisions; this led to the Congregational Church.
* Historians link early North/South differences to Chesapeake vs. New England colony contrasts.
* Differences stemmed from England's domestic issues: the Church of England demanded conformity, Puritans wanted reform, leading to persecution by 1620s.
* By 1640, New England had ~25,000 people; loyal Church members often went to Virginia for economic opportunity.
* English Civil War (1640s) between Royalists/Church supporters and Parliamentarians (Puritan-backed). Charles I executed in 1649; England became a republic in the 1950s.
* Puritans in New England sometimes returned to England for the war; Chesapeake colonists feared Puritan actions. Imperial oversight weakened during turmoil, letting regions develop different cultures.

---

**Revised Chapter (Dyslexia-Friendly & Readable)**

Some English people who stayed in England wrote about North America.  
They said the English would find great wealth there.  

These writers hoped to make money.  
They wanted raw materials from America.  
They wanted new places to sell English goods.  
They also wanted to spread Protestantism.  

But the English people who actually traveled to America had different reasons.  

In the Chesapeake Bay area, migrants started Virginia and Maryland.  
Their main goal was business.  
Early settlers at Jamestown first looked for gold.  
But they soon learned tobacco grew well there.  
Growing tobacco was the surest way to earn money.  
Thousands of young English men came to work in the tobacco fields.  
Many were unmarried, unemployed, or eager for change.  
A smaller number of English women also went.  

A very different group went to New England.  
They went because of religion.  
Many were Puritans.  
They often brought their wives and children with them.  
They followed their ministers across the ocean.  
They called this moving "beyond the seas."  
They wanted to build a new society based on their Protestant faith.  
They hoped it would be a good example for other Christians.  
They saw it as a place to oppose Catholic influence.  

While people in Virginia and Maryland worked on tobacco farms,  
people in New England built towns around churches.  
Each local church group decided its own rules.  
This is how the Congregational Church began.  

Many historians think the big differences between North and South in the United States started with these two colony types.  
The Chesapeake colonies and the New England colonies were very different from the start.  

These differences came from problems inside England itself.  
In the early 1600s, the official English church – the Church of England – required people to follow its rules exactly.  
Puritans wanted more changes in the church.  
By the 1620s, leaders of the Church of England saw Puritan preachers and their followers as dangerous.  
They thought Puritans threatened the king and national security.  
As church rules became stricter, many Puritans decided to move to New England.  
By 1640, about twenty-five thousand people lived in New England.  

Meanwhile, loyal members of the Church of England often went to Virginia.  
They went for economic opportunity.  
Some also mocked or laughed at Puritans both in England and in America.  

Big troubles broke out in England in the 1640s.  
This was a civil war.  
Royalists supported King Charles I and the Church of England.  
Parliamentarians were the reformers, often backed by Puritans.  
In 1649, Parliamentarians executed King Charles I.  
In the 1650s, England became a republic – it had no king.  

English colonists in America paid close attention to these events.  
Some Puritans left New England and returned to England to join the fight against the king.  
Other English people in Virginia and other colonies were afraid of what the Parliamentarians might do.  
They saw great danger in the actions of the Puritan-led forces.  

The war and chaos in England made it hard for officials in England to control the American colonies.  
It was difficult to send orders or enforce rules across the ocean.  
Because of this, the Chesapeake region and New England each developed their own unique culture.  
They became more different from each other over time.  

---

Complex sentences are broken into multiple short ones. *Example: Original "Promoters of English colonization in North America, many of whom never ventured across the Atlantic, wrote about the bounty..." becomes "Some English people who stayed in England wrote about North America."*

    *   "promoters/boosters" → "some English people who stayed in England / writers"
    *   "bounty" → "great wealth / find great wealth"
    *   "commercial orientation" → "their main goal was business"
    *   "determinedly commercial" (implied) → "Their main goal was business"
    *   "reformed Protestantism would grow and thrive, providing a model..." → "They wanted to build a new society based on their Protestant faith. They hoped it would be a good example for other Christians."

### Chapter: From Indentured Servitude to Racial Slavery in the English Colonies

**Early Shifts in the West Indies**  
English colonies first used enslaved Africans as their main labor force in the West Indies.  
Barbados was colonized by England in the 1620s.  
At first, planters grew tobacco there.  
By the 1640s, they switched to growing sugarcane.  
They began relying more and more on enslaved Africans for this work.  

In 1655, England took control of Jamaica from Spain.  
Jamaica quickly became a profitable sugar colony.  
Forced labor ran the plantations there.  
This served England’s growing empire.  

**Slavery in the Chesapeake (Virginia and Maryland)**  
Slavery spread more slowly in the Chesapeake colonies—Virginia and Maryland.  
By the end of the 1600s, both colonies used chattel slavery as their main labor system for tobacco.  
Chattel slavery legally treated Africans as property, not as people.  
Colonists in the Chesapeake also enslaved Native peoples.  

**Early Years: Africans Before Slavery**  
The first Africans arrived in Virginia in 1619.  
Slavery did not exist in England at that time.  
It was not yet an institution in colonial America.  
Many Africans worked as servants, like White people did.  
Some Africans who converted to Christianity could own their own land.  
Some of these African landowners even had White servants working for them.  

The status of Africans in the Chesapeake changed toward enslaved people in the last decades of the 1600s.  

**Bacon’s Rebellion and Its Impact**  
Bacon’s Rebellion happened in Virginia starting in 1674.  
It was an uprising by both White people and Black people.  
They believed the Virginia government blocked their chance to gain land and wealth.  
They also thought the government did little to remove Native Americans from the land.  

The rebellion is named after Nathaniel Bacon.  
Bacon was a wealthy young Englishman who arrived in Virginia in 1674.  
He first had a friendly relationship with Governor William Berkeley.  
But Bacon felt excluded from the governor’s important circle.  
Bacon wanted land on Virginia’s frontier.  
Governor Berkeley refused to allow more expansion, fearing war with Native tribes.  

Many of Bacon’s followers were former indentured servants.  
They believed Berkeley limited their chances for economic success.  
They felt denied the right to own tobacco farms.  
Bacon’s group thought Berkeley’s frontier policy did not protect English settlers enough.  
Worse, in their view, Berkeley signed treaties with local Native peoples to keep peace.  
Bacon and his followers saw all Native peoples as obstacles to getting land.  
They wanted to exterminate Native peoples.  

Tensions between English colonists and Native peoples led to war.  
In 1675, Susquehannock warriors attacked frontier settlements.  
They killed English planters and destroyed plantations, including one owned by Bacon.  

In 1676, Bacon and other Virginians attacked the Susquehannock without the governor’s order.  
When Berkeley ordered Bacon’s arrest, Bacon led his followers to Jamestown.  
They forced Governor Berkeley to flee to Virginia’s eastern shore for safety.  
Then they burned Jamestown.  

A civil war followed. It was called Bacon’s Rebellion.  
It was a violent conflict between supporters of the governor and supporters of Bacon.  
News of the rebellion reached England.  
King Charles II sent royal troops and English commissioners to restore order in Virginia.  
By the end of 1676, those loyal to the governor won.  
They executed several rebel leaders.  
Bacon himself escaped execution. He died later that year from dysentery.  

The rebellion ended in 1676. But deep divisions remained in Virginia.  
Supporters of Bacon still held grievances about access to Native lands.  

**How Bacon’s Rebellion Changed Slavery**  
Bacon’s Rebellion helped speed up the creation of a system of racial slavery in the Chesapeake.  
At the time of the rebellion, indentured servants made up most laborers in the region.  
Wealthy White people worried about this large group of workers.  
They feared the freedom indentured servants sometimes had.  
They also worried about the alliance Black and White servants formed during the rebellion.  

Replacing indentured servitude with racial slavery reduced these worries.  
It lessened reliance on White indentured servants, who often felt dissatisfied or caused trouble.  
It created a group of laborers defined strictly by race.  
Their movements were tightly controlled.  
It also made it harder for Black and White workers to unite again in the future.  
Racial slavery even helped ease tensions between rich and poor White people.  
Now, they could feel united as members of a group seen as “superior.”  

**New Laws After the Rebellion**  
Colonial laws in Virginia and Maryland had already made slavery legal before Bacon’s Rebellion.  
But new laws passed right after the rebellion took away more freedom for Black people.  
These laws helped build racial slavery.  

Virginia passed a law in 1680. This law did three things:  
* It forbade free Black people and enslaved people from carrying weapons.  
* It banned Black people from gathering in large groups.  
* It set harsh punishments for enslaved people who attacked Christians or tried to escape.  

Two years later, in 1682, Virginia passed another law.  
This law said: All Africans brought to the colony would be enslaved for life.  

The growing use of enslaved people in tobacco colonies—and the strict laws controlling them—did two things:  
1. They helped planters meet their labor needs.  
2. They made English colonists feel safer.  
3. They lessened fears of more uprisings.  
4. They reduced class tensions between rich and poor White people.

### chapter: from indentured servitude to racial slavery in the english colonies  

**early shifts in the west indies**  

english colonies first used enslaved africans as main labor in the west indies.  
barbados was colonized by england in the 1620s.  
at first planters grew tobacco there.  
by the 1640s they switched to sugarcane.  
they began relying more and more on enslaved africans for this work.  

in 1655 england took jamaica from spain.  
jamaica quickly became a profitable sugar colony.  
forced labor ran the plantations there.  
this served englands growing empire.  

**slavery in the chesapeake virginia and maryland**  

slavery spread more slowly in the chesapeake colonies virginia and maryland.  
by the end of the 1600s both colonies used chattel slavery as main labor for tobacco.  
chattel slavery legally treated africans as property not as people.  
colonists in the chesapeake also enslaved native peoples.  

**early years africans before slavery**  

the first africans arrived in virginia in 1619.  
slavery did not exist in england at that time.  
it was not yet an institution in colonial america.  
many africans worked as servants like white people did.  
some africans who converted to christianity could own land.  
some of these african landowners even had white servants working for them.  

the status of africans in the chesapeake changed toward enslaved people in the last decades of the 1600s.  

**bacons rebellion and its impact**  

bacons rebellion happened in virginia starting in 1674.  
it was an uprising by both white people and black people.  
they believed the virginia government blocked their chance to gain land and wealth.  
they also thought the government did little to remove native americans from the land.  

the rebellion is named after nathaniel bacon.  
bacon was a wealthy young englishman who arrived in virginia in 1674.  
he first had a friendly relationship with governor william berkeley.  
but bacon felt excluded from the governors important circle.  
bacon wanted land on virginias frontier.  

governor william berkeley refused to allow more expansion fearing war with native tribes.  

many of bacons followers were former indentured servants.  
they believed berkeley limited their chances for economic success.  
they felt denied the right to own tobacco farms.  
bacons group thought berkeleys frontier policy did not protect english settlers enough.  

worse in their view berkeley signed treaties with local native peoples to keep peace.  
bacon and his followers saw all native peoples as obstacles to getting land.  
they wanted to exterminate native peoples.  

tensions between english colonists and native peoples led to war.  
in 1675 susquehannock warriors attacked frontier settlements.  
they killed english planters and destroyed plantations including one owned by bacon.  

in 1676 bacons group attacked the susquehannock without the governors order.  
when berkeley ordered bacons arrest bacons followers went to jamestown.  
they forced governor william berkeley to flee to virginias eastern shore for safety.  
then they burned jamestown.  

a civil war followed it was called bacons rebellion.  
it was a violent conflict between supporters of the governor and supporters of bacon.  
news of the rebellion reached england.  
king charles ii sent royal troops and english commissioners to restore order in virginia.  
by the end of 1676 those loyal to the governor won.  
they executed several rebel leaders.

the rebellion ended in 1676 but deep divisions remained in virginia.  
supporters of bacon still held grievances about access to native lands.

at the time of the rebellion indentured servants made up most laborers in the region.  
wealthy white people worried about this large group of workers.  
they feared the freedom indentured servants sometimes had.  
they also worried about the alliance black and white servants formed during the rebellion.  

replacing indentured servitude with racial slavery reduced these worries.  
it lessened reliance on white indentured servants who often felt dissatisfied or caused trouble.  
it created a group of laborers defined strictly by race.  
their movements were tightly controlled.  
it also made it harder for black and white workers to unite again in the future.  
racial slavery even helped ease tensions between rich and poor white people.  
now they could feel united as members of a group seen as superior.

colonial laws in virginia and maryland had already made slavery legal before bacons rebellion.

these laws helped build racial slavery.

it forbade free black people and enslaved people from carrying weapons.  

it banned black people from gathering in large groups.  

it set harsh punishments for enslaved people who attacked christians or tried to escape.  

two years later in 1682 virginia passed another law.  
this law said all africans brought to the colony would be enslaved for life.

Here is a revised version of the chapter written to be clear, concise, and accessible for readers with dyslexia or other reading challenges. It uses short sentences, plain language, concrete terms, and avoids complex structure while preserving all factual content and meaning. Key differences and protections are explicitly stated in simple terms.

**Original Source: Robert Beverley, *History and Present State of Virginia* (1705)**

Robert Beverley was a wealthy planter in Jamestown, Virginia. He also enslaved Black people. His writing shows clear differences between White servants and enslaved Black people.

**How Beverley Described Servants and Enslaved People:**

*   Servants could be White people. They had contracts called indentures. These set how long they must work (usually a few years).
*   Enslaved people were Black people and their children. Law said they were enslaved for life. This was based on the mother's status: *partus sequitur ventrem* (the child follows the womb). So, if a woman was enslaved, her baby was also enslaved.
*   Both groups worked in the fields. They tilled soil, manured land, sowed and planted tobacco, corn, and other crops.
*   There were differences in clothing and food between them.
*   Work tasks for field laborers were similar, no matter their status. Overseers, free people, and planters gave orders.

**Key Differences in Legal Protection and Treatment:**

1.  **Time of Service:**
    *   Enslaved people (and their children) were enslaved for life. Their service had no end date.
    *   White servants served for a fixed time. This depended on their contract or the law if they had no contract.
    *   If a White servant was under 19 years old, a court decided their exact age. They then worked until they turned 24.
    *   If a White servant was over 19 when first brought to court, they only served 5 years.

2.  **Treatment of White Women vs. Enslaved Women:**
    *   It was rare or not done to force a White woman to work out in the fields (in the ground).
    *   The law put heavy taxes on any White woman who *did* work in the fields. This discouraged it. All other White women were free from this tax.
    *   In contrast, it was common to make an enslaved woman work outside in the fields. The law did not give her any special protection or different tax treatment based on where she worked (abroad or at home).

3.  **General Legal Status:**
    *   Servants (White) had a defined period of service ending by age or time. They could become free after that period.
    *   Enslaved people (Black and their children) were legally bound for life. Their children were automatically enslaved too, no matter where they were born.

**Answering the Questions Based on Beverley's Text:**

*   **According to Robert Beverley, what are the differences between the servants and the enslaved?**  
    Servants (who were White) served for a limited time (by contract or law), could become free after that time, and had legal protections about working in the fields (especially for White women). Enslaved people (who were Black and their children) were enslaved for life, their children were also enslaved automatically, and they had no guaranteed end to their service. There were differences in clothing, food, and expected work roles, especially for women.

*   **What protections did servants have that enslaved people did not?**  
    Servants had a defined period of service (ending by age or years) after which they became free. White women specifically had legal protection from being forced to work in the fields (with heavy taxes discouraging it), while enslaved women had no such protection and were commonly worked outside. Servants also had clear court processes to determine their age and service time if they had no contract, ensuring they weren't over-serviced beyond the law. Enslaved people had none of these legal protections regarding time of service, freedom, or restrictions on where women could be forced to work.

**New England in the 1600s**

The English colonized two main areas early in the 1600s. One was New England. It started differently from the tobacco colonies in Virginia and Maryland. Those places focused on making money. New England began with religion.

Puritan families mainly settled New England in the 1630s. They came because of their faith. In England, people had wanted church changes since the 1580s. These reformers followed John Calvin’s Protestant ideas. They were called Puritans. They believed the Church of England needed to remove things not found in the Bible, especially old Catholic practices.

Many early New England leaders were trained ministers. They studied at Cambridge or Oxford. But because they questioned church rules, the king and his officials stopped them from having jobs. This was to stop dissenting views. Other Puritan leaders, like John Winthrop (first governor of Massachusetts Bay Colony), were wealthy landowners (gentry).

Puritans left England for several reasons. They did **not** go to create a place where *all* religions were free. Instead, they wanted to practice *their own* religion without being punished. In their "New" England, they tried to build a community that followed Bible teachings as they understood them. They aimed to create a model of reformed Protestantism—a new English Israel.

Puritan beliefs caused conflict in England. They opposed traditional customs and fun activities. For example, they spoke against bear baiting (dogs attacking a chained bear), often done on Sundays when people had free time. In the age of Shakespeare’s plays, Puritans wanted to close theaters, calling playhouses immoral places. The Bible itself was part of the conflict with King James I. Soon after becoming king, James ordered a new Bible version. He wanted to stop Puritans from using the Geneva Bible (which followed Calvin and put God above the king). The King James Version, printed in 1611, stressed the king’s power and glory.

By the 1620s and 1630s, conflict grew. The state church banned Puritan ministers from preaching. Church leaders saw Puritans as a threat to national security. Their demands for religious, social, and cultural change challenged the king’s authority. Many unwilling to follow the Church of England left for America.

But not all who moved to America agreed on everything. Some wanted to completely leave the Church of England. Others still hoped to reform it from inside. They both settled in New England during this time.

The Glorious Revolution changed England. It led to a government where the king had less power. It also gave protections to English people.

In October 1689, William and Mary became king and queen. That same year, the 1689 Bill of Rights was made. This created a constitutional monarchy in England.

*   The right to freedom of speech in Parliament.
*   The right to hold regular elections.
*   The right to ask the king for changes (to petition the king).

*   The right to a trial by jury.
*   The right to habeas corpus. This means authorities must bring an imprisoned person before a court. They must show the reason for the imprisonment in court.

In 1690, Locke published his Two Treatises of Government. In it, he argued that government is an agreement between leaders and the people. He said representative government exists to protect three things: life, liberty, and property.

Locke rejected the idea of the divine right of kings. He did not believe kings get their power only from God. Instead, Locke supported a central role for Parliament. He advocated for a monarchy with limited power.

The 1773 Tea Act made colonists worried again.  
Patriots in the Sons and Daughters of Liberty saw the act as proof that some corrupt members of Parliament were breaking British government rules.  
People who had protested before often thought British actions were part of a big plan against freedom.  
So they felt the 1773 act was part of that plan too.  

Colonists answered the Tea Act with a boycott, as they had for earlier taxes.  
Groups called Committees of Correspondence helped organize resistance in colonial port cities along the East Coast.  
Because of this, British ships carrying tea could not come to shore to unload their cargo.  
In Charlestown, Boston, Philadelphia, and New York, large amounts of tea stayed locked in warehouses or rotted in ship holds.  
Ships had to return to Great Britain without unloading.  

Thomas Hutchinson was royal governor of Massachusetts by then.  
He said radicals like Samuel Adams would not stop the ships from unloading tea.  
Hutchinson urged local merchants to accept the tea once it was unloaded.  
The ship *Dartmouth* arrived in Boston Harbor in November 1773.  
It had twenty days to unload its cargo and pay the tax before sailing back to Britain.  
Two more ships, the *Eleanor* and the *Beaver*, arrived soon after.  

Samuel Adams and the Sons of Liberty tried to stop ship captains from paying the tax.  
They posted people around the ships to keep the tea from being unloaded.  
On December 16, as the *Dartmouth*'s deadline ended, many townspeople met at the Old South Meeting House in Boston.  
From this meeting, a group of Sons of Liberty and their followers went to the three ships.  
Some people dressed as Mohawk community members.  
A crowd protected them.  
They emptied all the tea into the harbor.  
The destroyed tea was worth almost one million dollars in today’s money. This was a very large loss at the time.  
This event inspired more acts of resistance up and down the East Coast.  

Not all colonists supported dumping the tea.  
Many Patriots did not agree with destroying property either.

**Women's Roles During the American Revolution**

Women in colonial America had many important home duties. They cared for children and managed the household. The war for independence made their work harder. In some ways, it also kept their roles clear.

Husbands and sons left home to fight. Women then had more to do at home. They also had to help the army directly. Women produced items for the war effort. These included clothing and food. They kept their own homes running while doing this.

Women were often asked to give food and shelter to soldiers. They also nursed wounded men after battles.

The Revolution did open new public roles for some women. An informal group called the Daughters of Liberty formed around 1765. They worked hard to support the war effort against British taxes.

Esther DeBerdt Reed lived in Philadelphia. Her husband was Governor Joseph Reed. She started the Ladies Association of Philadelphia. This group raised money for the Continental Army. They bought supplies the soldiers needed.

In 1780, Esther wrote a letter to other women. She said: *"The time has come to show the same feelings we had at the start of the Revolution. Then, we stopped using tea, even though we liked it, because it came from our enemies. We showed them we thought basic needs were more important than comforts when our freedom was at stake. Our hard-working hands spun flax and made linen for the soldiers' use. When we were exiles or fugitives, we faced all the hardships of war with courage."*

Esther Reed and other Philadelphia women raised almost $300,000 in Continental money for the war effort. This was a large sum that greatly helped the army.

> The United States government under the Articles of Confederation had serious problems, especially with trade between states.

> **The Philadelphia Convention of 1787**

> The official reason for the Philadelphia meeting was to change (amend) the Articles of Confederation. But the attendees decided very quickly to do something different. They agreed to create a completely new plan for a national government.

> This new plan became the United States Constitution. Because of this, we now call this meeting the Constitutional Convention of 1787.

> Fifty-five men came to Philadelphia. They met in secret. We know what happened because James Madison wrote careful notes of each day’s talks.
> 
> The delegates knew their work would be controversial. Rhode Island had not sent anyone. New Hampshire’s delegates arrived later than the others.

The American Revolution ended British rule in the United States.  
Some people supported the new 1787 Constitution. They were called Federalists.  

Federalists had views about society similar to those in Britain before the war.  
They did not form a political party right away. Instead, they shared some main beliefs.  

One belief was that only people with property could take part in politics.  
This meant many citizens could not vote or hold office.  

Federalists also believed the Revolution had not changed social roles.  
They thought traditional roles between women and men stayed the same.  
They thought traditional roles between White people and other races stayed the same.  

Federalists believed there were clear ranks and differences in intelligence.  
To them, the idea that all people are equal seemed unreasonable.  

They argued that women, Black people, and Native peoples had lower status than White men.  
They said these groups must know their place as secondary to White male citizens.  
They feared trying to make everyone equal would harm the new republic.  
The United States was not set up to be a pure democracy.  

The people who wrote the Constitution led the new government.  
Most members of the first national government were Federalists.  
George Washington became president. He appointed Federalists to top jobs:  
*   Alexander Hamilton was Secretary of the Treasury.  
*   Thomas Jefferson was Secretary of State.  
*   Henry Knox, who fought with Washington in the Revolution, was Secretary of War.  
*   Edmond Randolph, a Virginia delegate at the Constitutional Convention, became Attorney General.  

In July 1789, Congress passed the Judiciary Act.  
This law created the Supreme Court. It had six justices. All were supporters of the new government.  

Congress passed its first major law in 1789: the Tariff Act.  
This law put a tax on goods coming into the country.  
The goal was to raise money for economic problems.  
Nationalists, who wanted a strong federal government, supported this.  
They had tried similar laws during the Confederation in the 1780s but failed.  

The Tariff Act also set a duty of fifty cents per ton of cargo on foreign ships.  
This tax was based on materials carried, not the ship's weight.  
This policy gave American ships and goods a commercial advantage.

**Work before factories was different.**  
Farmers chose when to do tasks. An artisan could take an afternoon off if he wished. A farmer could rebuild his fence on Thursday instead of Wednesday. Workers talked during the day. Many journeymen received alcohol as part of their pay. One person might read a book or newspaper aloud to others. In warm weather, doors and windows were often open. Work stopped when it became too dark to see clearly.

**Work in factories was very different.**  
Employees had to arrive at a set time. This was usually early in the morning. They worked all day. They could not leave when tired. They took breaks only at set times. Workers who arrived late lost pay. Being 5 minutes late could cut many hours of pay. Repeated lateness could lead to being fired. The same tasks repeated over and over made days feel long. Most factory workers labored ten to twelve hours each day. They worked six days each week. In winter, the sun set early. Oil lamps lit the factory floor. Workers strained their eyes to see. Smoke from the lamps filled the rooms. Workers often coughed because of the smoke. In spring, as days got longer, factories held "blowing-out" celebrations. This marked when oil lamps were turned off. These blow-outs often had processions and dancing.

Drinking was not allowed. Some factories did not let workers sit down. Doors and windows stayed closed. This was especially true in textile factories. Breezes could disturb fibers. Workers were given more machines to tend. Owners made machines run faster. Wages were cut in many places. Workers who once earned by the hour now often did piecework.
